10387-a-century-too-soon-the-age-of-tyra:
John R. Musick published this historical romance in 1909, as volume six of his Real America in Romance series. Its subject is Bacon's Rebellion in Virginia, a century before American independence, when colonists first stirred against royal rule. Musick calls the age one of tyranny, yet full of early republican feeling.

Cavaliers and Puritans, Quakers and Catholics, divide the colony, while brave, gallant, and sober settlers clash over power and faith. The sleeping goddess of liberty, Musick says, opened her eyes, then slept again for a hundred years. Readers get a vivid, period tale of colonial revolt.
1246-the-house-of-dust-a-symphony:
Conrad Aiken, an American poet, builds this long poem as a symphony in four movements. Voices speak from a house of dust: lovers, dreamers, and the dead, all passing through rooms of memory. The poem moves in waves of image and music rather than in story.

Aiken's lines are lush and dreamlike, full of sea, wind, and light, and the poem's form was bold for its day. It won praise as a landmark of modern American verse. The book suits readers who like poetry that works like music, with mood carrying the sense.
13043-william-of-germany:
William of Germany, by Stanley Shaw, published in 1913, traces Kaiser Wilhelm II from youth through his reign to 1913. Chapters follow his boyhood, the years before he took the throne, the accession of 1888, the court, and the break with Bismarck known as dropping the pilot. Later sections cover Morocco, the November storm of 1908, and the emperor as he stood in 1913.

Bismarck's public replies in the Hamburg News show the clash at the heart of the book, above all over the 1890 deal that gave Germany Heligoland for Zanzibar. Shaw's life of the Kaiser remains a useful early English portrait of a ruler whose choices shaped Europe.
13664-selections-from-the-writings-of-lo:
Selections from Lord Dunsany's writings, 1912, gather The Gods of the Mountain, the first act of King Argimenes and the Unknown Warrior. The Fall of Babbulkund, The Sphinx at Gizeh, Idle Days on the Yann, A Miracle, and The Castle of Time. Lady Wilde's tale of a Dublin crowd opens the book, as a young girl escapes into a shop.

Agmar questions a man who saw gods terrible in the gloaming, green and not as they now appear, while children who saw them died. Travellers journey south through desert to an oasis of palms by a well, watering haughty camels, resting in shade, and singing songs of Babbulkund. Dunsany's prose is dreamlike, ornate, and strange, building whole mythologies in a few pages.
13800-the-pleasures-of-a-single-life-or-:
Printed in London in 1709 for one penny, this satire praises single life and mocks matrimony. It claims occasion from divorces lately granted by Parliament. Verse opens with wedlock as a cursed, uncomfortable state, cause of woes and object of hate. The speaker recalls calm joys before fatal cares oppressed him.

A companion piece, The Choice, praises pleasures of a country life. The satire addresses beaus against the next vacation, urging them to stay free. Its humour is coarse and of its age, with talk of dying convicts torn between fear and reprieve. The pamphlet suits students of Restoration and Augustan satire. It also shows early print culture at street price.
14233-over-strand-and-field-a-record-of-:
Gustave Flaubert's record of travel through Brittany, published in Chicago in 1904, begins at Chambord. Empty galleries and deserted rooms show spiders spinning over Francis the First's salamanders. Poverty here has no grandeur, Flaubert writes: floors repaired in one room rot in the next, in futile effort to preserve what dies. Conscious poverty brushes its threadbare coat and tries to look respectable.

Coast walking follows. Cliffs crowd, pile, and overturn, and travelers slide on slippery rock while a swallow cuts luminous air above them. Bear-baiting supplies a brutal interlude: dogs cling to a bear's back, men bite dogs to loosen jaws, and a mattock frees one bulldog's grip. Dust settles on spectators as beasts gasp and men pull hairs from their teeth. Flaubert's eye stays pitiless and poetic, finding beauty and cruelty side by side on the Breton shore.
14407-the-tale-of-benjamin-bunny:
Beatrix Potter's 1904 picture book brings back Peter Rabbit's cousin Benjamin, who slips into Mr. McGregor's garden to rescue Peter's lost clothes. The tale, written for the children of Sawrey, follows the earlier Peter Rabbit story.

Benjamin and Peter dodge the cat, hide under baskets, and climb down a pear tree into lettuce beds, leaving small footmarks everywhere. Potter's watercolor scenes of garden, wall, and wood carry much of the charm. The book is short, gentle, and funny, and it remains one of the best-loved entries in her animal tales.
15977-frank-and-fanny:
A rural story for children by Mrs. Clara Moreton, issued by Phillips, Sampson and Company in Boston in 1851, entered in 1850. Numerous engravings join the text. Moreton's preface states her purpose plainly: to inculcate gentleness, patience, and benevolence, and to inspire the young with love for simple rural pleasures.

Frank and Fanny live a country childhood of fields, chores, and kind deeds. Exciting narratives, Moreton warns, do not favour the mild virtues, which she calls the most beautiful ornaments of character. Her tale keeps its pace gentle and its lessons clear. The book gives a mid-century ideal of childhood: quiet, good, and happy in the country.
16040-kenny:
Leona Dalrymple's novel Kenny, illustrated by Joseph Pierre Nuyttens and printed in Chicago in 1917, follows a household of strong-willed people in a country setting. Chapter titles trace the action: Brian rebels, a cabin in the pines, a blossom storm, a miser's will and gold, Kenny's truth crusade, and Kenny's ward. Joan, Adam Craig, and a chair by the fire all take their place in the story.

The book mixes family quarrels, romance, and mystery with a warm, outdoor feeling, moving from spring weather to a shadow of death and back toward hope. Dalrymple, known for Diane of the Green Van, writes lively, popular fiction for general readers. Kenny offers a pleasant, old-fashioned tale of youth, pride, and second chances.
1646-roads-of-destiny:
O. Henry gathers short stories around chance and choice. The small turn that changes a life drives the title tale, following a young shepherd who leaves home after a quarrel and faces three different roads. The collection moves between Texas ranches, city rooms, and village streets, and its people are clerks, cowboys, lovers, and drifters.

What holds the stories together is O. Henry's trick of the late reversal: a plan collapses, a stranger proves to be someone else, or a kindness lands where it was least expected. Readers who like plot-driven tales with a sting in the last page will find the author's best-known manner here, in short, self-contained form.
16779-a-ryght-profytable-treatyse-compen:
Thomas Betson wrote this short profitable treatise, drawn from many writings of holy men, printed in Caxton's house by Wynkyn de Worde about 1500 and reprinted at Cambridge University Press in 1905. It is one of twenty-six tracts once bound together in a volume given to Cambridge in 1715 by King George I with Bishop John Moore's library. Betson's name comes only from the colophon.

The treatise gathers short counsels for a devout life, in the plain, pious style of late medieval England. Its reprint keeps old spelling and marks for modern readers. The book gives a rare glimpse of what ordinary holy folk read around 1500, short, practical, and meant for daily use rather than for scholars.
17141-destiny:
Charles Neville Buck's 1916 novel opens in a White Mountains schoolhouse, where a slight thirteen-year-old boy broods apart from his mates. Part One, called The Land of Promise, follows his youth, his dreams, and the pull of a wider life beyond the hills. Autumn maples, chestnuts, and schoolroom drones set a vivid, almost dreamy scene for his start.

Buck writes in rich, romantic prose, with fate and choice as twin threads through the hero's growth. The book suits readers who like old-style tales of a poor boy, a hard start, and a life shaped by will and chance. Its first part alone gives a full sense of the boy, his place, and his hopes.
17928-the-influence-of-india-and-persia-:
Arthur F. J. Remy wrote The Influence of India and Persia on the Poetry of Germany in 1901, printed by Columbia University Press in New York. Remy, a fellow in comparative philology at Columbia, dedicates the study to his teachers William Carpenter and Calvin Thomas.

Chapters trace what medieval Europe knew of India and Persia, then follow Portuguese voyages, Persian studies, and the slow arrival of Indian lore in German letters. Remy shows how Eastern tales, images, and faiths seeped into German verse. The book is a learned, early study of East-West letters, still useful for students of that rich exchange.
18632-crossroads-of-destiny:
H. Beam Piper wrote this short story for Fantastic Universe in July 1959. Its narrator, a college history teacher, keeps a dollar bill in his bank box as proof of a strange night, afraid to show it even to fellow teachers. In a train club car he hears five men debate how history might shift if Columbus had sailed under the English flag of Henry VII rather than Spain.

One of the men takes notes for a planning staff, hinting the talk is more than idle fancy. Piper plays the what-if with a straight face, letting small choices loom large. The story is a neat early example of alternate-history fiction, short, sly, and easy to read in one sitting.
18948-damn-a-book-of-calumny:
H. L. Mencken published this short book in New York in 1918, in a third printing from Philip Goodman Company. It is a string of brief, sharp pieces on subjects that run from patriotism and art to humor, lying, war, actors, clubs, and marriage. Each item runs only a page or two, and the table of contents reads like a list of targets.

Mencken's method is attack by aphorism: a bold claim, a quick example, and a sting in the tail. He mocks moral indignation, praises the artist against the crowd, and doubts most respectable opinion. Readers get Mencken at his most combative and quotable, a good short introduction to the critic who shaped American newspaper wit in the 1920s.
19017-tales-of-destiny:
Edmund Mitchell wrote this 1913 book of tales told by Indian narrators, from a Rajput chief to a fakir, a merchant, and an Afghan general. Each tale turns on fate, stars, or a vow, and each teller speaks in his own voice. The frame is a circle of storytellers in Mughal India.

One tale follows Rukpur Singh, chief of Jhalnagor and captain of Akbar's guard, into battle with elephants, matchlocks, and falling rocks. Others deal with diamonds, tigers, and a mother's love. Readers get rich, old-style Eastern tales where destiny rules and courage meets its price.
19565-bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-and:
Laura Lee Hope wrote this children's book about Bunny Brown, his sister Sue, and their Shetland pony; its New York printing appeared in the late nineteen teens with pictures by Thelma Gooch. It belongs to a long series that took the pair to farms, circuses, camps, and city homes.

Here Toby the pony carries them over a ford on a smooth gravel bed, then clattering back over a bridge, while the children talk over their good time. The book's simple pleasures, animals, water, and roads, made it a steady favorite with young readers.
2023-malvina-of-brittany:
Jerome K. Jerome collects short comic stories here, led by the title tale of Malvina of Brittany, a strange visitor whose coming unsettles a quiet household. A doctor who doubts the story still admits it changed how he sees life. Jerome wrote these stories between his famous comic novels, keeping the same easy voice for shorter work.

Other pieces include a street with a blank wall, an evening out, a lesson, and a pair of fawn gloves, each told with Jerome's dry humor. The tales mix the everyday with a touch of the uncanny, and none takes itself too seriously. The uncanny touches stay light, since Jerome prefers a laugh to a chill, and his ghosts seldom mean real harm.
21304-begumbagh-a-tale-of-the-indian-mut:
George Manville Fenn fills this volume with a long tale and three shorter stories. It starts with Begumbagh, about a small British garrison holding out during the Indian Mutiny. A one-armed narrator tells it, holding his sliding paper down with a lead inkstand. Suspense, Fenn's trademark, drives every chapter.

The second story concerns cursed gold plate in an old gentleman's house, and the curse proves real. The third traps two smugglers in a gowt, a sea drain cut in eastern England. The last follows a fine new ship through an Atlantic storm after her captain takes to drink and a junior officer takes command.
22319-mezzerow-loves-company:
Mezzerow Loves Company is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its scene opens with a welcome to Earth. An official greets newcomers arriving from the outer worlds.

He can spot fresh arrivals by one small sign. Their eyes lack the identifying gleam that marks everyone else. On principle, he would stamp one woman's passport with dull and dingy ink. That petty detail gives the future world its bureaucratic chill. The story builds its strange society out of stamps, eyes, and quiet dread. Readers meet a compact tale about belonging, papers, and being marked as an outsider on sight.
22774-barbara-in-brittany:
Barbara in Brittany is a children's story of an English girl's stay in Brittany, the Celtic corner of France. The catalog record names no author and gives no year. Travel tales for girls of the era mixed mild adventure with lessons in foreign custom, and Brittany, with its pardons, costumes, and coast, was a favorite ground.

The sample catches a small moral moment: Barbara holds little Lucy in her lap and coaxes her out of shyness. You won't run off the moment she speaks to you, will you, Lucy? It's rude, you know. Try to answer nicely when she wants you to. French hosts, strange food, and new friends presumably test both girls further. The book offers a gentle tour of Brittany through a child's eyes, manners included.
23500-the-car-of-destiny:
C. N. and A. M. Williamson wrote this nineteen hundred seven Spanish romance, dedicated to Dona Maria del Pilar Harvey and pictured by Armand Both. Lady Monica, the heroine, moves through a tale of a king's car, a guest who was not asked, a mystery over a chauffeur, and a chase over the border.

A stern pursuit, a balcony scene, a cathedral, a duke changed, a secret of the king, and a thief in the night follow. Maria del Pilar comes to the rescue, with moonlight in the palace of the kings. The Williamsons mix motor touring, court intrigue, and love with their usual verve. Readers who like romantic adventure with a Spanish flavour will enjoy the car's winding road from puzzle to happy close.
24124-down-the-rhine-or-young-america-in:
Oliver Optic, the pen name of William T. Adams, wrote this travel adventure for young readers, published in Boston in 1870. It is the sixth and last book of the first Young America Abroad series, closing the Academy Squadron's first voyage to Europe. The students and their friends leave their ships for an excursion into Germany.

The tale mixes sights, travel mishaps, and boyish adventure along the Rhine, meant to teach as well as amuse. Earlier books in the series had taken the same party through Ireland, England, Holland, France, and Switzerland. Readers get a brisk schoolboy tour of German towns, rivers, and roads in 1870.
2470-samuel-brohl-and-company:
Victor Cherbuliez's Samuel Brohl and Company follows a Jewish adventurer in Paris who reinvents himself as a count, chasing wealth and a wife among the high society he deceives. The novel's satire cuts both ways: Brohl's imposture exposes the snobbery of those he fools. Cherbuliez writes with a French novelist's polish and irony.

The book was a great success in its day, praised for its wit and its social observation. Its treatment of its hero now invites critical reading. Readers of French fiction will find a lively, provocative novel. Cherbuliez was a member of the French Academy and a popular novelist.
25880-american-poetry-1922-a-miscellany:
Printed by Harcourt, Brace and Company in 1922, this miscellany gathers new American verse without tying it to one school or theme. A foreword recalls the stir caused by the first such volume in 1920, when readers kept asking who had edited a book that claimed no editor. The new book again refuses a single label, be it nature, love, patriotism, propaganda, or philosophy.

The table of contents runs from Amy Lowell, Robert Frost, Carl Sandburg, and Vachel Lindsay to James Oppenheim and Alfred Kreymborg, among others. Poems range from plain speech to bold experiment, with city voices, country voices, and a colophon that shouts its new America across plains and peaks. The set gives a wide, lively snap of verse in the early nineteen twenties.
26760-memories-of-bethany:
The Reverend John R. Macduff, author of Morning and Night Watches and Memories of Gennesaret, published these Bethany meditations with Robert Carter and Brothers at New York in 1861. Macduff inscribes them to mourners in Zion, for whom Bethany has always meant sorrow made holy.

Opening passages gather every Bethany reference in the sacred narrative. They run from Martha receiving Jesus into her house while Mary sits at his feet to Lazarus, sick at Bethany, dead four days, and raised. Martha meets Jesus on the road, confessing him as the Christ, the Son of God, while Mary sits still in the house. Chapters run from opening thoughts and the home scene through the messenger, the message, and the sleeper to the mourner's comfort, the mourner's creed, and the master.
27229-brother-bosch-an-airman-s-escape-f:
Captain Knight's Brother Bosch, an airman's escape from Germany, published by Heinemann in 1919, tells of capture and escape in the First World War. Dedicated to Captain Morritt, Lieutenant Medlicott, Lieutenant Walters, and all who gave their lives in the endeavour, it keeps the camp spelling Bosch for local colour.

Knight's fellow prisoners include Wolfe, commonly known as the Worm, and a second lieutenant forever on the prowl, never knocking before entering a room. The memoir moves from prison camp routine to the plans, risks, and luck of getting out, in a plain airman's voice.
27377-a-little-maid-of-massachusetts-col:
Alice Turner Curtis, author of A Little Maid of Province Town and A Little Maid of Narragansett Bay, wrote this girls' story of colonial Massachusetts. It was published by the Penn Publishing Company of Philadelphia in 1915 with illustrations by Wuanita Smith. Its young heroine Anne lives among family, friends, and neighbors in the colony.

Chapters follow Amanda's mistake, Anne's decision, a visit with the Mashpees, and a stay at Brewster. They go on to a black-bearded man, a disappearance, a trip to Boston, a strange schooner, and a great adventure, ending homeward bound. Curtis mixes everyday colonial life with mild peril and friendship. Young readers get a gentle, old-fashioned historical tale.
2811-letters-of-pliny:
Gaius Plinius Caecilius Secundus, known as Pliny the Younger, wrote these letters, here translated by William Melmoth and revised by F. C. T. Bosanquet. Born at Como in 62 AD, Pliny was eight when his father died, and he was adopted by his uncle, the elder Pliny, author of the Natural History.

The letters cover law, friendship, villas, and the eruption of Vesuvius, which killed his uncle. Pliny writes with polish, curiosity, and Roman civic pride. The collection remains a priceless window on imperial Rome, and a model of the familiar letter as literature.
28268-the-countess-of-albany:
Vernon Lee wrote The Countess of Albany in 1910, second edition, as a life of Louise, Countess of Albany, wife of Charles Edward Stuart, the Young Pretender. Lee, dedicating the book to a late friend, follows Louise from bride and bridegroom through Florence, Rome, and Colmar, to her salon and her final years at Santa Croce. Portraits illustrate the volume.

Chapters treat her escape, her separation, her years with Alfieri, and her circle of writers and artists. Lee writes with sympathy and care for sources. The biography suits readers of eighteenth-century history who want a woman's life at the centre of Jacobite romance.
28432-home-life-in-germany:
Mrs. Alfred Sidgwick's Home Life in Germany, first published in 1908, looks at German daily life from inside the home rather than from official reports. The author states plainly that she offers no statistics on taxes or building laws. She knows instead how German women spent their days.

Chapters cover children, schools, the education of the poor, girlhood, marriages, householders, housewives, servants, and town life. The result is a friendly, observant portrait of Germany before the First World War. It is valuable now as a record of customs, family routines, and attitudes that later histories rarely describe at close range.
29338-england-and-germany:
E. J. Dillon published this study of England and Germany in 1917, with an introduction by William Morris Hughes, prime minister of Australia. Dillon dedicates the book to Princess Alice of Monaco, calling it a partial presentment of the beginnings of a world cataclysm. Writing during the First World War, he seeks the roots of the conflict.

Chapters cover the character of Germany, its system of preparation, Italian finance, the annexation mania, Germany and Russia, and the statesmanship of the Entente. Later chapters treat Teuton politics, propaganda in Scandinavia, and the Balkans. Readers get a wartime analysis by a well-informed observer, partisan in tone but rich in the diplomacy and rivalries that led to war.
29934-the-auburndale-watch-company:
Edwin A. Battison, associate curator of mechanical and civil engineering at the Smithsonian's Museum of History and Technology, wrote this paper as number four in the museum's Contributions series. Its subtitle calls it the first American attempt toward the dollar watch. Battison based the study on the patent model of the Auburndale rotary and other company products in the National Museum, with other collections, including his own.

Five sections order the tale: The Invention, Developing the Invention, The New Sponsor, Success and Failure, and The Lesson. The dream was a machine-made watch with interchangeable parts, long in men's minds, crowned near Boston but missed at Auburndale. Careful digging brought to light the design and manufacturing errors behind the failure. The paper is a clear, short history of a bold, failed first try.
2995-tacitus-on-germany:
Tacitus wrote On Germany, in Thomas Gordon's translation, as a study of the Germanic peoples beyond Rome's frontier. Tacitus was probably born about 54 AD and died after 117, a friend of the younger Pliny, an advocate and orator, and the son-in-law of Agricola, conqueror of Britain. His short work describes tribes Rome knew mainly through war. The text records customs that struck Roman readers as strange.

Children were nourished with their own mothers' milk and never handed to nurses, and lords lived undistinguished from slaves, among the same cattle on the same ground. Free-born youths part from the rest when bravery recommends them. The Germania remains a key Roman source on northern Europe.
30386-the-one-and-the-many:
Milton Lesser tells The One and the Many, a short tale asking the one question: what lies beyond the ultimate? Some call the war foolish, and the narrator's brother said so in the Sunset Country. His brother, lame, does nothing but sketch star pictures, joining stars with lines as in a child's puzzle to make fish, archer, and hunter shapes. That, the narrator says, is foolish.

Perhaps it started it all, since he gazed at the stars hunting for pictures instead of minding his sentry post. Taken, with a hand from the darkness clamped over his mouth and a blade pricking the small of his back. He first feared the camp would be slain as it slept. The Onists, twenty archers against their outpost, had other ideas, and took him away on a night run through woodlands.
30464-a-manifest-destiny:
Julia Magruder writes A Manifest Destiny, illustrated and published in New York and London in 1900, following her earlier Magnificent Plebeian. Illustrations show Bettina throwing back her veil, sinking back in her chair, and hearing questions about a handsome boy, money partly her own, and the very spirit of widowhood.

Chapter one opens with Bettina Mowbray walking the deck of an ocean steamer bound for England, aware that many eyes watch her with interest. She studies their glances as closely as they study her, since being noticed by men and women of the world matters greatly to her. Magruder blends society romance with a heroine's keen sense of rank and reputation.
30798-sonny:
Rick Raphael wrote this science fiction story, printed in Analog in April 1963, about a hill boy in uniform and the strange power of a thought. Private Jediah Cromwell, new to the Army, feels homesick for the first time since he left the almost cut-off West Virginia hills of his birth. Back home, his mother Ma Cromwell feels trouble coming down the trail, in the shape of Cletus Miller, unseen since just before her husband died.

The tale links those two worlds, barracks and hollow, through a gift that seems to bend what thought alone can do. Raphael tells it in plain, folksy speech, with Jed's mother reading the hills as keenly as any scout. Readers get a short story about home, family, and a power no one can quite measure, told with warmth and a touch of mountain humor.
30871-legends-romances-of-brittany:
Lewis Spence, a fellow of the Royal Anthropological Institute, wrote this book of legends and romances of Brittany, published by Frederick A. Stokes in New York, with thirty-two pictures by W. Otway Cannell. Spence had already written Hero Tales and Legends of the Rhine, a dictionary of medieval romance, and myths of Mexico and Peru. His Brittany book moves from land and people to the old stones, fairies, and saints of the region.

Thirteen chapters treat menhirs and dolmens, fairies, sprites and demons, world-tales, Breton folk-tales, popular legends, hero-tales, the black art, Arthurian romance, the lays of Marie de France, saints, and costumes and customs. A glossary and index close the book. Pictures include Graelent and the fairy-woman, Merlin and Vivien, and fairies of Broceliande. It is a rich, old-fashioned guide to Breton lore.
31408-the-oxford-degree-ceremony:
J. Wells, a fellow of Wadham College, Oxford, wrote this short study of the Oxford degree ceremony, published by the Clarendon Press in 1906. Six chapters take the reader through the ceremony itself, its meaning, and its history, with attention to the forms, dress, and language that mark each stage. Wells writes as an insider explaining a ritual most visitors see only from outside.

The book's value lies in that explanation: it connects present practice to older custom and shows why each part of the ceremony survives. Students of Oxford, of academic ritual, or of English university life will find a clear, compact guide. It reads as both a handbook for the occasion and a small history of one of Oxford's most public traditions.
31737-the-sloths-of-kruvny:
Vern Fearing's short story was printed in Amazing Stories in October and November 1953. It is billed by its headnote as a very unserious yarn, offered because a sense of humor seems the only salvation in a grim world of atom bombs and worsening television commercials. Its hero is Bradley Broadshoulders, called Brad or Broad or Shoulders, an obese youth in the green tunic of the Galaxy Patrol.

Brad stands grim-lipped, as is the custom of spacemen, waiting for his commander, Metternich, known also as Foxey Gran'pa, to speak fateful words. Readers get a comic space story that sends up heroic postures, with a hero who has a tidy crop of Venusian fungus and no shred of muscle.
31922-felony:
James Causey's short story Felony, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction in July 1954, follows a man named Vogel from childhood puzzles to man's greatest enigma. At nine, Vogel nearly killed another boy who scattered his half-finished jigsaw puzzle; at sixteen, the mysteries of the Danish Gambit moved him to tears.

At twenty-two, crouched in a foxhole on Okinawa, Vogel ignored death bursting about him to work on a tattered newspaper crossword. At thirty he managed production at Sachs Fixtures, tall, gaunt, and ruthless. Readers get a darkly comic tale of a pattern-seeking mind, for whom every system, from puzzles to crime, is a problem waiting to be solved.
32525-the-curlytops-at-uncle-frank-s-ran:
Howard R. Garis's Curlytops book, copyrighted in 1918, takes the Curlytops to Uncle Frank's ranch, subtitled Little Folks on Ponyback. Chapters open with Trouble's tumble, Nicknack and Trouble, off for the west, and a collision, followed by arrival at Ring Rosy Ranch and cowboy fun. Bad news, a queer noise, a sick pony, and a surprised doctor follow, with Trouble making a lasso.

Later chapters bring a bucking bronco, missing cattle, looking for Indians, Trouble helping, a trail, and the Curlytops alone. Julia Greene's illustrations accompany a story of ranch work, ponies, and family fun, in Garis's familiar series manner. Young readers get western adventure without harshness, as small children learn ranch manners and help, sometimes too eagerly, with real work.
32676-the-test-colony:
Winston Marks sends a test colony to Sirius XXII, a world reached after a dreary two-year voyage from Earth. Leader Phillip Benson and recorder Sam walk a sandy beach and meet two naked natives, male and female, who prove to be no stowaways from their own party.

The natives have four digits and no thumbs, long prehensile toes, and silky hair, and they watch the newcomers with frank curiosity. As contact grows, trade in a local fruit drink, broken quarantine rules, and a failure to check native births test Benson's plan to keep his colony from going native.
33052-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
This slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica gathers the entries running from Camorra to Cape Colony. Its articles include the Camorra, Campania and its Campagna, Tommaso Campanella, the Campbells from Alexander to Sir Henry Campbell-Bannerman, Cannae, Cannes, cannibalism, and Canning. Shorter entries on plants, places, and terms in the same alphabetical span sit alongside them. Transcriber's notes record corrections to articles on Canaan, cantata, and Cape Colony.

The slice mixes history, biography, geography, and natural science in the confident voice of early twentieth-century reference writing. Readers get the facts and judgments educated readers of the day were expected to trust, from a secret society to a colony's climate. As a reference text it is dated, but as a record of how knowledge was ordered a century ago, it remains a useful window on the period's mind.
34223-the-new-germany:
George Young's 1920 book The New Germany reports on Germany from the Armistice to the Treaty of Versailles. Young went to Berlin in January 1919 as a correspondent for the Daily News, and wrote most of the book in the summer of that year.

Seven chapters trace revolution, reaction, council republics, ruin and rebuilding, council rule, the treaty, and the new constitution. Young asks two plain questions: how far the German people had truly turned against Prussianism, and whether a lasting peace could be built on reform. Young adds an index, and his chapters run from the revolution to the new constitution in order.
34232-from-kingdom-to-colony:
Mary Devereux wrote From Kingdom to Colony, for Little, Brown in 1904. Rights were held in 1899 by that Boston house. Sandham drew the pictures, one showing Dorothy with George Washington. Devereux gives the book to her father, with a tombstone's praise. Eminent in life and noble in heart, the inscription runs.

A prologue opens in 1066, when William of Normandy invaded England. Robert of Evreux, a younger son, came with the Conqueror. His name stands on the Battle Abbey roll in many spellings, she notes. The tale then opens on a May day in 1639, under Charles the First. On a May day in Warwick, far from war or court rumours, it idles. Bromwich Castle, home of Sir Walter Devereux, stands in the scene. Devereux follows her name from Norman roll to American colony.
34397-a-short-history-of-germany:
A Short History of Germany is a survey by Mary Platt Parmele, published by Scribner in New York in 1898 as one of her short histories of the nations. Parmele states her method in the preface: it matters more to comprehend the forces that created a nation and the steps of its unfolding than to know every event along the way.

She warns that she has kept to the main line of development and resisted details that do not bear on it, leaving the bypaths for later. The chapters run from the Indo-European migrations and Hermann's defeat of Varus through Charlemagne, Canossa and Barbarossa, to Luther, the Augsburg Confession and beyond. The Gothic kingdoms, the Hanseatic League, the Golden Bull and the invention of printing all find their place on the main road. It is history as a single clear line, drawn for the general reader.
34790-perverted-proverbs-a-manual-of-imm:
Streamer, a colonel by his pen name, wrote this book of comic verse, published in New York in 1903. The title page calls it Perverted Proverbs, a manual of immorals for the many. Streamer also wrote Ruthless Rhymes for Heartless Homes and Ballads of the Boer War, which sets the tone for the jokes to come.

A long verse dedication to Helen Whitney opens the book. In it the poet thanks her for praising his earlier rhymes and offers these lines in return. A short foreword warns that the press may cry that he corrupts the young, and says he stays unmoved by such taunts. Readers get old sayings twisted for laughs, in light verse.
36478-the-red-year-a-story-of-the-indian:
Louis Tracy wrote a novel of the Indian Mutiny of 1857. The book came out in New York in 1907. Tracy also wrote The Wings of the Morning and The Pillar of Light. His hero is named Malcolm in the part heads. The tale starts in January 1857 at Dum-Dum, near Calcutta.

A sepoy with Brahmin marks sits by a well in camp. From that seed the revolt grows to Delhi and Cawnpore. Parts deal with a well of death, a road to Lucknow, and a king's court. A woman steps in at key turns. The close brings a price paid for sin and strife.
36576-the-student-life-of-germany:
The Student Life of Germany, by William Howitt, was issued at Philadelphia in 1842 from an unpublished manuscript by Doctor Cornelius. Howitt had written The Rural Life of England and The Book of the Seasons. The book holds near forty of the most famous student songs of Germany. A motto calls youth a golden time that comes not again.

German students of that age lived by codes of honour, song, and the duel. Howitt sets their world before English and American readers in full. Burschen songs, drinking customs, and university towns fill the pages. The songs are given as the heart of the life described. Readers get a foreign student world in its own proud voice. The book is both a travel study and a songbook of the German universities.
37360-object-matrimony:
Montague Glass wrote Object: Matrimony, a work of comic fiction first under copyright in 1909 and issued in book form in New York in 1912. Glass builds his scenes out of talk: New York business men haggle, plead, and scheme in richly accented speech. The book opens in the world of real estate at a bad moment in the market.

Philip Margolius, owner of four double flat-houses with every flat standing empty, begs his lawyer, Henry Feldman, for a scheme to beat his second mortgage holder. The houses sit ten blocks from the nearest trolley, and Margolius swears they could not be given away. Feldman, a careful lawyer with a name in Democratic politics, hears him out while a subway line is still only a promise. Readers get Glass's dry comedy of debt, hope, and fast talk, in which every talker has an angle and every promise costs money.
39118-the-christian-creed-or-what-it-is-:
Annie Besant wrote a freethought pamphlet printed at London in 1883, promising to show errors, contradictions, and absurdities given on divine authority in the Old Testament. A struggle has begun, she opens, which promises to be one of the fiercest this century has seen. Bigots and persecutors stand on one side, supporters of free speech on the other. It is worth looking closely, she says, into the creed that claims the right to imprison men for non belief.

Christianity threatens persecution here and damnation hereafter, Besant charges. He that believeth not shall be damned, she quotes against it. The pamphlet followed the blasphemy prosecutions of freethinkers. Besant was then Charles Bradlaugh's ally in the secular movement.
39899-star-the-story-of-an-indian-pony:
Star, the Story of an Indian Pony, was written by Forrestine C Hooker and published by the Sun Dial Press of Garden City, New York, in 1922. Lieutenant-General Nelson A Miles wrote the introduction, and Charles Livingston Bull painted the jacket picture. The tale is told by the pony himself, a son of Running Deer, swiftest racer of the Comanche ponies.

Star belongs to Songbird, the little daughter of Quannah, chief of the Quahada Comanches, and he loves her above all else. In his introduction Miles quotes his own report to General Sheridan of November 1874 on the wild herds and their riders. The book gives young readers the plains wars from a pony's side of the camp, where loyalty to a small mistress rules the story.
4024-the-man-of-destiny:
A one-act play sets a young general at an inn during the Italian campaign, where a lady of rank and beauty enters with the poise of one used to privilege. Her flowered silk dress, Watteau pleat, and creamy fichu mark her station, while the innkeeper greets her with natural good manners.

Talk turns to dispatches, secrets, and the game of war, as the general finds his plans crossed by a woman as quick as he is. The play is a duel of wits in a single room, with history as its backdrop. Readers get a brisk, witty piece about power, charm, and the moment when a great man's fate hangs on a small exchange.
40608-mitz-and-fritz-of-germany:
Mitz and Fritz of Germany, a travel story for children by Madeline Brandeis, was copyrighted in 1933 by the A Flanagan Company and issued by Grosset and Dunlap. Photographs carry the book: town and church views were shot in Germany itself. Child actors play the parts, Mitzi Green as Mitzi Toymaker and Jackie Searle as Fritz. A pet dog poses as Frankfurter.

The Toymaker family leaves Nuremberg and tours the land. Chapters stop at Bayreuth, Mainz, and Bonn, where Beethoven is the theme. Hamelin brings the old piper tale, and Eisenach brings Bach. A castle and the poet city follow, then the Leipzig fair and a concert. Fritz and his violin thread the trip together. Brandeis dedicates the book to her German schooled father.
40792-behind-the-scenes-in-warring-germa:
Behind the Scenes in Warring Germany is Edward Lyell Fox's report from inside Germany in the First World War. McBride, Nast published it in New York in 1915. Fox was a special correspondent with the Kaiser's armies and in Berlin. A picture shows him with a captain of Hindenburg's staff after a battle.

Chapters open at the threshold of war and visit the west front. Fox flies on the back of the bird of war and spends a night before Ypres. He reports the trenches, captured Belgium, and prisoners of war. On the eastern front he follows the Russian retreat and the battle of Augustowo Wald. The book closes by asking the future: peace or war.
41594-the-disputed-v-c-a-tale-of-the-ind:
The Disputed V C is a tale of the Indian Mutiny by Frederick Gibbon, with drawn plates by Stanley Wood. It is a boys book in a press set of such tales. The front plate shows a man drop a lit wick on a thin trail of blast dust. Past twenty parts trace one young flag man past the great revolt.

Ted Russell, flag man of a Bengal foot corps, is sour and cross on the first day of the year of the revolt. That year brought vast woe to homes past two lands, the tale says. Parts take in the burst of the revolt, a fight in the arms store, a house held past siege, and the relief of a famed town. A cheat corps, a foe chief, and a choice by a friend drive the plot.
42279-the-great-company:
Beckles Willson wrote this history of the Honourable Company of Merchants-Adventurers trading into Hudson's Bay. Dodd, Mead and Company published it at New York in 1900, with an introduction by Lord Strathcona, the company's governor. Willson dedicates the annals to Sir Wilfrid Laurier, to whose suggestion and encouragement he says the compilation is largely due.

His preface argues that elementary studies must precede any unified Canadian history, and that the company is such a coherent unit. It watched French dominion in North America rise and vanish, new British colonies planted, and those colonies quarrel with the parent state and become states themselves. Through two full centuries of unceasing change, he writes, the Hudson's Bay Company endured unshorn of its greatness, the one enduring pillar in the New World mansion. Maps, plans, and drawings by Arthur Heming illustrate the book.
42484-the-popham-colony:
Printed in Boston in 1866, a set of newspaper pieces argues over the worth of the Popham Colony and what the old claims for it can prove. The colony was an English landing at the mouth of the Kennebec River in 1607. Each year since 1862, crowds had marked the day with speeches that praised the landing.

William Frederick Poole attacked those claims in print, and Edward Ballard and Frederic Kidder wrote back in sharp reply. The book gathers the full exchange in the order it ran, piece by piece. A list of books and papers on the subject ends the volume for readers who want more.
42866-rambles-in-brittany:
Francis Miltoun wrote a travel book dated 1905 on rambles in Brittany, with prints by Blanche McManus. The book grew at a small inn in a fishing town, where the host kept watch on its birth for weeks. Miltoun calls it a set of trips by road and rail round the coast, not a full survey.

Towers, church art, and shore towns pass in a loose and fond string of scenes. The aim is to add to the dry stock of guide books, not to swap them out whole. A mate book on Normandy and works on great churches of France and the Rhine share the same rich art and care.
42954-brittany:
Brittany is a travel book with pictures by Mortimer Menpes and text by Dorothy Menpes. Adam and Charles Black published the work at London, first in 1905 and again in 1912. The book belongs to a series of colour plate travel volumes. Other volumes in the series treat Japan, Venice, India, and China.

The contents tour the Breton coast and its old towns one by one. Chapters visit Douarnenez, Vitre, Vannes, and Quimper, then Saint Malo and Mont Saint Michel. Colour plates show fisher folk, markets, and cottage kitchens. The text opens at Douarnenez, a grey fishing village that wakes when the boats come home. The clatter of wooden shoes down steep, bad paved streets tells of the fleet's return. The closing chapter sums up Brittany as a romantic land.
4349-wisdom-and-destiny:
Maurice Maeterlinck wrote this essay on wisdom and destiny, translated by Alfred Sutro and dedicated to Georgette Leblanc. What began as a short piece of twenty pages, meant for a fortnight's work, grew over more than two years into a full volume. Maeterlinck calls it kin to his Treasure of the Humble, but different in treatment.

Where the earlier book speculated like a poet athirst for beauty, this one seeks truth like an earnest thinker. Maeterlinck asks how wisdom changes fate, and whether a life lived inwardly can meet outward chance. The essay suits readers of reflective prose who enjoy slow argument over quick advice.
4376-sowing-seeds-in-danny:
Nellie L. McClung wrote this Canadian novel about Mrs. Burton Francis, a dreamy woman with beautiful theories, and her silent husband. Camilla Rose, a capable young woman, looks after the household and sometimes helps apply those theories. The Watson family, including Pearl, an imaginative girl of twelve, works on the section and washes for the Francises.

McClung dedicates the story to her mother, with verses on kindness as what the old world needs. The novel tests Mrs. Francis's ideals against prairie life in Danny, where theory meets work, neighbors, and need. It is a warm, humorous book about good intentions, and about the people who must live with them.
43970-every-day-life-in-the-massachusett:
Every Day Life in the Massachusetts Bay Colony, by George Francis Dow, first came out at Boston in 1935 and was reissued by Arno Press at New York in 1977. The first head is the sea trip. Francis Higginson's word to those who would come is to pack meal, malt, cloth, tools, iron, and glass. No mart waits on the far shore. Then the home takes shape: first lean shelters, then framed houses, and the goods that filled them.

Counterpanes, dress, and pewter get heads of their own. Farm, manners, sports, and trades fill the mid run. Coin runs from wampum to paper, herb tea stands for the doctor, and crimes and their pains close the tale. Old shop lists in the back give the goods by name and price. Past fans get the Puritan day in full dress.
44100-ruth-of-boston-a-story-of-the-mass:
Ruth of Boston, a story of the Massachusetts Bay Colony by James Otis, was copyright in 1910. Ruth tells the tale in her own voice. She crossed from London to America at the age of twelve, a rare trip for a girl, and writes it down for her old age, and for any who find her book.

Long contents map the first years of the colony in small steps. Ruth sees Salem, picks a home, and moves to Charlestown, then to the town of Boston. She tells of famine, the great sickness, and the ship Lyon that brings food. She tells of flax work, soap, schools, and harsh laws. She tells of Roger Williams in flight and of war with the Pequot. Young readers get colony life day by day, through a girl's eyes.
44147-the-great-american-pie-company:
Ellis Parker Butler wrote The Great American Pie Company, a humorous tale copyrighted in 1904 and published in New York in 1907. Butler was the author of Pigs Is Pigs. Will Crawford drew the pictures. The story is set in Gloning, a town the narrator maps onto a pie cut in two by Mud River.

On the East Side lives Mrs. Deacon, a fat, good-natured woman whose famous pies built her a trade. Her husband Ephraim, a deep thinker who scorns labor, delivers them from the back steps where he prefers to sit. On the West Side lives Mrs. Phineas Doolittle, painted as a base imitator of the Deacon pies. Butler builds his comedy on the rivalry, in the tall-tale manner that made him a favorite American humorist.
45721-by-order-of-the-company:
By Order of the Company, by Mary Johnston, was published at Westminster by Archibald Constable in 1900, the year of its American copyright. Johnston's earlier romance, The Old Dominion, fills the front pages with praise from the Guardian, the Tablet, Punch, and the Daily Telegraph. The chapter titles run in old style, each beginning with the words In Which.

The tale opens with a throw of dice, meets Master Jeremy Sparrow, and marries its teller in haste. Jamestown follows, with a fight against the Spaniard prepared and a lost lady sought. A haunted wood, a trial, and guests of an emperor fill the later chapters.
46865-war-days-in-brittany:
Elsie Deming Jarves wrote War Days in Brittany, a collection of her personal experiences in the Great War, published at Detroit by the Saturday Night Press in 1920. France had already thanked her: the silver medal of the Reconnaissance Française came to her by decree of the President, for devotion to the wounded in Brittany since the war began. Her husband was made a Chevalier of the Legion of Honor for the same cause.

Jarves dedicates the book to the generous Americans whose money helped the work through. A letter at the front, from a member of the Institut de France, shows the price French families paid. Of his four young nephews, three fell on the field of honor. The fourth, an aviator in Russia, won three citations. American readers get a relief worker's Brittany, recorded by the woman France decorated.
47576-the-moon-colony:
William Dixon Bell wrote The Moon Colony, copyrighted in 1937. Thirty-one chapters open Bullet Proof, then The Stowaway, An Arctic Blizzard, and A Flashing Cylinder. Down into the Den and A Dangerous Scientist follow.

Ready to Crush Out Life, Billy Takes a Part, and Start to the Moon build the launch. Toplinsky calls the bluff, tables turn with no eats, and the landing comes at chapter thirteen. A moon army, battling with crickets, and Billy disappearing fill the middle. Chapter one opens with Julian Epworth reasoning that his departure from Salt Lake City is a profound secret, an airship carrying gold his easy job. Readers get a boys' science fiction novel of moon war by cricket and ramph.
48028-the-metaphysic-of-christianity-and:
The Metaphysic of Christianity and Buddhism is a work of comparative religion by Dawsonne Strong. Watts and Company published it in London in 1899. Strong was a major-general, late of the Indian Army. He dedicates the book to his wife, in memory of their sojourn in the East.

The subtitle calls the work a symphony, and its chapters pair the two faiths. Jesus and Gotama are set side by side in the opening chapter. God and the kosmos, then soul and karma, follow in the comparison. Heaven and nirvana form the fourth great pairing of the scheme. Concluding remarks and a temple visit in Ceylon round out the argument. The introduction faces the difficulty fairly at the start. A sincere Christian, Strong notes, struggles to grant equal holiness to another faith.
48539-a-system-of-pyrotechny:
A System of Pyrotechny is a work on fireworks and their warlike kin by James Cutbush, published at Philadelphia in 1825. Cutbush had taught chemistry and mineralogy at the military academy at West Point. The book is built in four parts. The first treats the substances used in fireworks. The second gives the instruments, tools, and hand work of the art. Fireworks for exhibition fill the third. Military pyrotechny closes the set.

The title page names the readers aimed at: the military and naval officer, the man of science, and the artificer. Cutbush was a member of the American Philosophical Society and of learned bodies in Philadelphia. His sister Clara published the book after his death. It is the first full American treatise of its art, part chemistry and part craft manual.
49207-anno-domini-2000-or-woman-s-destin:
Anno Domini 2000, or Woman's Destiny is a novel of the future by Sir Julius Vogel, published by Hutchinson in London in 1889. Vogel dedicated it to the Earl of Carnarvon for his work in consolidating the Canadian dominions. A prologue set in 1920 lays the ground in present misery.

George Claude Sonsius loses his post after an accident cripples his right hand, and his family sinks into an attic in one of London's poorest neighbourhoods. His crippled son lies on a horsehair mattress in pain, short of food and care. From that ground the book jumps to the year 2000 and a United Britain. Hilda Fitzherbert stands at the centre of the later story, with Lord Reginald Paramatta and an emperor planning campaigns. Chapters promise cabinet negotiations, heroine worship, air-cruisers, and a grateful Ireland. An epilogue rounds off the prophecy.
49366-selections-from-cassell-company:
Selections from Cassell and Company Publications is a publisher catalogue of books on offer. Art, the Magazine of, in yearly volume form, leads the list of fine art books. Five hundred choice engravings fill that yearly volume at sixteen shillings. After London, a tale by Richard Jefferies, stands next in the roll.

A life of Prince Bismarck in two volumes with two portraits follows at twenty four shillings. The life and times of John Bright and a set of British ballads come after. British Battles on Land and Sea, in three volumes with some six hundred pictures, holds a place. European butterflies and moths, with sixty one coloured plates, serves the nature shelf. Victorian book buyers browsed new titles by price and plate count in lists like this.
49509-my-escape-from-germany:
Eric Keith tells his escape from Germany in the Great War years. Century printed the book in New York in January 1920. A map shows the dotted route of his escape at front. Contents split the tale into three parts of tries and failures.

Part one opens in a cell on April 7 in 1916. Keith sat three miles from the Dutch frontier and freedom road. A fat German warder locked him in with a pleased smile. Ruhleben camp, a sanatorium, hiding, and fresh arrests fill his account. Free at last is the chapter that ends the long third part.
50882-introduction-to-the-study-of-pal-o:
John Hutton Balfour wrote a guide to the study of fossil plants, issued in 1872. Adam and Charles Black brought out the book at Edinburgh. Balfour taught medicine and botany at the University of Edinburgh. Four stone plates and more than one hundred wood cuts show the forms.

Balfour gave the book to Heinrich Robert Goeppert of Breslau, a famed fossil botanist. He holds that no one can judge fossils well without deep study of living plants. Tissue, growth, spread, soil, and climate all bear on the old forms. Students gain a firm start in a field then new in British schools.
51022-brittany:
Baring-Gould wrote Brittany for the Little Guides series, first published in 1902 and here in its third edition of 1921. The small volume carries pictures by Wylie, photographs, and three maps. Its preface is honest about the region: Brittany cannot claim to be a land of grand scenery, and its hills are insignificant beside true mountains.

The charm of Brittany, Baring-Gould argues, lies in its people and its churches. The people keep peculiar costumes and customs, best seen at a pardon, the patronal feast of some chapel. The churches, mostly granite, take carving of lace-like delicacy in the dark kersanton stone, which keeps its sharpness for centuries. Coast scenery shifts from the granite cliffs of Finistere to the sandy dunes of the Morbihan. Readers get a compact companion for travelers who value folkways and old churches over famous views.
51231-syndrome-johnny:
Syndrome Johnny is a science fiction story by Charles Dye, illustrated by Emsh, printed in Galaxy Science Fiction for July 1951. Its opening question frames the whole tale: the plagues that struck mankind could be traced to one man, but was he a fiend or a savior?

The story begins in a blood bank, where plasma is processed, frozen, and stored. A woman dies after a transfusion, and patients sicken with changed appetites, digestion, and moods. A hospital administrator traces the harm to nine travellers who sold their blood. One of them carries death in his veins, and a thumbprint hunt fails to find him. Three years on, the carriers seed an epidemic in four cities; three years later it circles the world, killing twenty-seven million of fifty million people before vanishing.
51572-in-good-company:
In Good Company, by Coulson Kernahan, was published in London in 1917. John Lane issued this second edition in London and New York. Its subtitle promises personal recollections of seven men. Swinburne, Lord Roberts, Watts-Dunton, and Oscar Wilde lead the list. Edward Whymper, Stone the hymn-writer, and Stephen Phillips follow. A letter at the front gives the book to Mrs Arthur Henniker. Kernahan recalls a shared friend whose hope joined them. Her husband the general, proud of her stories, is dead, and the book honours his memory too.

Swinburne opens the contents, with a sonnet dated April 10, 1909. Kernahan lunched with the poet at The Pines. Watts-Dunton takes four chapters by himself. Wilde gets a long late place. The book is literary London remembered by a man who sat at its tables.
51966-the-last-penny:
The Last Penny, by Edwin Lefevre, was published in New York and London in 1917. Thomas Leigh, called Tommy, is three days out of college. Chapter one finds him at home, weighing a dozen neckties before breakfast. His college triumphs were of charm, not of study. Invites crowd his summer: Gloucester, a Newport cruise, the Adirondacks, and Labrador game in the fall. Yet he stands at his last ten dollar bill.

His father sends exact sums by return mail and makes no fuss. The formal name Thomas keeps the boy in line, the narrator jokes. A talk about his allowance waits ahead. Lefevre, known for market tales, here draws a rich young man at the edge of real life.
52619-the-medici-balls-seven-little-jour:
Anna Sheldon and Moyca Newell wrote The Medici Balls, seven little journeys in Tuscany. Charterhouse Press put out the New York book in 1904, with over one hundred pictures. The rights were held that year by Newell, and the book is given to Frances Cecilia Newell. A portrait of Lorenzo de Medici fronts the volume. The opening note weighs a vexed question of heraldry: why the Medici took red balls on a field of gold.

One school holds that the balls are pills, since the name Medici means physicians. Saints Cosmo and Damian, patrons of medicine, stand in Medici votive pictures, they add. Others hold the balls were the old sign of money-lenders. Giovanni de Medici, founder of the greater branch, took the sign as a banker, they say. The journeys then roam the towns and halls of Florence's great house.
53074-professor-johnny:
Professor Johnny is a book for young readers by an author who signed only the name Jak. Thomas Crowell of New York held the copyright in 1887. Johnny earns his nickname from his glasses and his love of study. He performs small trials in natural philosophy and chemistry, and his young friends call him the Professor.

His merry little sister Sue teases him to stop reading and play. Chapters promise an illustrated lecture, a sky room, an unwelcome guest, and lessons from nature. One chapter gives Pierre's story, and others take the children to a cottage and a harbor. The book mixes home scenes with simple science. It shows a bright boy whose book learning is always being pulled back into family life.
53600-breton-folk-an-artistic-tour-in-br:
Henry Blackburn wrote Breton Folk, an artistic tour in Brittany, with one hundred seventy illustrations by R Caldecott, issued in Boston by James R Osgood and Company in eighteen eighty one. The notes grew from three summer tours in Brittany, two with the artist at his side. J D Cooper engraved the plates with utmost care. A Cavaliers and Roundhead plate heads the tour.

Breton Folk is not a book of antiquities nor of folk lore, the preface says plainly. The sketches show a black and white country in summer, a sombre land under white clouds. Peasants wear dark costumes with wide white collars and caps. Black and white cattle and magpies dot the fields. Chapters run from St Malo and Dinan through Lamballe, Guingamp, and Morlaix to Brest, Quimper, and Vannes. Travellers get a truthful, pictured Brittany of farms and coasts.
53987-marjorie-dean-macy-s-hamilton-colo:
Pauline Lester wrote Marjorie Dean Macy's Hamilton Colony, copyrighted in 1930 by the Burt Company at New York. The book belongs to the Marjorie Dean post-graduate series, for girls of twelve to eighteen. Earlier series followed Marjorie through high school and college.

Something fine is going to happen, Jerry Macy declares from the porch rocker, squinting at the August sky. Marjorie lists what has not happened. The Captain is late home from the beach. Letters from Leila and Vera are owed. Hamilton Arms stands boarded up, with no sign of Miss Susanna or Jonas. Jerry trusts her hunch anyway: someone unexpected will come, or be heard from.
54540-daughters-of-destiny:
Daughters of Destiny is a novel of adventure by Schuyler Staunton, published in Chicago in 1906. Staunton had earlier written The Fate of a Crown. The catalog title is clipped, but the title page gives the full name.

The tale is told in two books, The Man and The Woman. It opens in London, where Prince Kasam of Baluchistan argues with the financier Lord Marvale, who teases him that Englishmen know his country only from school geography. The chapters move between an American commission, a Persian physician, and the daughter of a vizier. Later chapters bring a capture, a veiled woman, an abduction, a chamber of death, and a rescue by Ahmed Khan. Eastern courts, harems, and secret plots drive the story.
54724-folk-tales-of-breffny:
Hunt gathered these folk tales of Breffny, an Irish border county. Macmillan printed the book in London in 1912 with a word list. The King's Daughter of France opens the set of twenty six tales. A widow cow, Kate Ellen wake, and a dark oath follow.

Fairy gold, an enchanted hare, and a child and fiddle appear. A new deck of cards, a voice at the door, and fairies come. Tales end with a churn story, a brogue maker, and gold digging. An old poor man and a red capped boy open tale one.
56120-pop-guns-one-serious-and-one-funny:
Aunt Fanny, in life Fanny Barrow, wrote this first book of her Pop-Gun series for Sheldon of New York. Pop-Guns, one serious and one funny, carries a dogs' dinner party as a plate. She gives the whole series to Thomas Lincoln, the president's son.

Shoot folly as it flies, her motto bids, under Richter's word: I love God and little children. A Pop-Gun Letter from Aunt Fanny opens the book. About the Children follows, then how Philip Badboy became Philip Wiseman. The dog's dinner and more small tales fill the rest. Five more Pop-Gun books stand listed behind it, from One Big Pop-Gun to Post-Office Pop-Guns. Civil War era tales for the nursery shelf.
56707-bertrand-of-brittany:
Bertrand of Brittany, by Warwick Deeping, published in 1908 by Harper and Brothers, is a historical novel of medieval France. Three books trace youth and the Silver Swan, how a man may find his soul again, and the Oak of Mivoie. The tale opens in the Breton lands at the hall of Sieur Robert du Guesclin.

His wife Jeanne, proud and handsome, grieves that her firstborn Bertrand is an ugly, fierce, crooked child, nothing like the Roland she dreamed of. Deeping builds his romance on that shame and the boy's slow rise. The book is rich in period color, heraldry, and the rough honor of a fighting age.
56937-christmas-on-the-briny:
Christmas on the Briny, also titled The Innocents Abroad, is a booklet by Christie, printed in 1909. It tells of a holiday trip to the Abrolhos Islands off Western Australia. The account first ran in the Geraldton Guardian, whose editor proposed reprinting it as a booklet. He hoped it might advertise the islands as a holiday resort, and Christie gave his permission.

A dozen or so residents of Geraldton, new and old, had asked what to do with themselves during the holidays. Someone suggested the Abrolhos, and the idea caught on. George Baston volunteered his fishing boat, the While-away, to take the party cruising round the islands. He also took charge of provisioning. All were to be aboard by midnight on Thursday, December 24. At twelve o'clock the cry of a merry Christmas was exchanged from shore to deck.
56951-battles-of-destiny:
Battles of Destiny is a history of seventeen decisive battles by Sister Fides Shepperson of Mount Mercy Convent, Pittsburgh. The book was sold at the convent and at the University Book Store for seventy-five cents, with copyright of 1914. Shepperson had already written Harp of Milan and Cloister Chords. The chapters are short essays, each on one battle that turned the fate of nations.

The roll runs the whole span of Western war. Marathon comes first, then Arbela and Zama. The Teutoburger Wald and Adrianople follow, then Chalons and Tours. Hastings, Orleans and Lepanto lead to the Spanish Armada. Naseby, Blenheim and Pultowa carry the story into modern times. Saratoga, Valmy and Waterloo close the list. Without it there would have been no Thermopylae, no Salamis, no Age of Pericles.
57099-miss-crespigny:
Miss Crespigny, by Frances Hodgson Burnett, was published by Charles Scribner's Sons at New York, copyright 1879. An advertisement for Mrs Burnett's earlier stories prices Lindsay's Luck and Theo at 30 cents and Kathleen and Pretty Polly Pemberton at 40 cents.

Burnett's author's note, dated October 1878, explains that these love stories first appeared in Peterson's Ladies' Magazine. Because the magazine was not copyrighted, the stories were issued in book form without her consent, dressed as her latest work. This edition, revised by her for the purpose, is the authorised one from her own publishers.
57235-prospectus-of-the-scots-new-zealan:
A prospectus for the Scots New Zealand Land Company was agreed at Perth on 24 August 1839 and ordered to be published. Patrick Matthew chaired the meeting of intending shareholders. William Gorrie moved the plan, and William Taylor seconded it. Scots in many parts of the country had already approved its main points.

The company's object is stated first. Shareholders' capital will carry them and their families to New Zealand, buy land and property there, and win protection and social advantages. The reasons for emigrating follow. A new country offers virgin soil at low prices and higher wages for labour. It is free of slavery, and nearly every man holds property. In Britain, by contrast, small capitalists watch their children sink as clerks and shopmen. The pamphlet sells emigration on land, wages, and room to rise.
57752-life-and-destiny:
Felix Adler, founder of the first Ethical Society, speaks in these talks on life and its fate. Watts printed Life and Destiny in London in 1913. The pieces are gems cut from Adler's addresses, as the publishers' note calls them.

The Meaning of Life opens the set, then Religion and Immortality. Moral Ideals and Love and Marriage take the middle. The Higher Life, Spiritual Progress, and Suffering and Consolation follow. An Ethical Outlook closes the book. Adler founded his New York society in 1876 and led it for decades. His creed put deed over dogma, and these talks press that faith on the great points of a human life.
58403-john-vytal-a-tale-of-the-lost-colo:
John Vytal is a historical novel by Payson, published by Harper and Brothers in 1901, subtitled a tale of the Lost Colony. The story reaches back to Elizabethan England and the Roanoke venture. Its opening pages linger on London Bridge, where a graceful young man leans against the barbican on an April afternoon.

The young man is Kit Marlowe, presented as a spring-tide force: dreamy-eyed one moment, brilliant the next, with a latent power that promises storm. The narrator insists the Elizabethan age is not dead history but quick and vivid, and pauses to paint Marlowe's dark, passionate face in detail before the plot begins. The portrait sets the novel's method: famous Elizabethans and colonial adventure woven into one romantic fabric, under mottoes from Marlowe and Fuller.
58470-diana-trelawny:
Diana Trelawny is a novel by Oliphant, in one book form for a cheap run of English tales. That run lists her past works at its front, most in two book forms. This form came out at Leipzig for sale in London in the early eighteen nineties.

Her past tales in that list take a rail man and his young, a wed tale, and a bird in the nest. A tale of the age in letters stands there as well. This tale opens with the girl her self, then her folk next door. A trip to Italy comes third, the road by which she will meet the man and the doom the tale has in store.
58642-whipperginny:
Whipperginny is a book of poems by Robert Graves, printed in Britain. Knopf of New York issued the American edition in nineteen twenty three. Graves gives the volume to Edward Marsh on its dedication page. Most poems cover three years from the New Year of nineteen twenty.

A few rhymes are older stock from nineteen eighteen, Graves note confesses. Henry and Mary, What Did I Dream, and Mirror Mirror date from then. That year he wrote Country Sentiment while fleeing a painful war neurosis. The Pier Glass mood was aggressive, but this book turns more detached. New problems in religion, mind, and belief grow in the later pieces.
58690-for-the-love-of-lady-margaret-a-ro:
William Thomas Wilson wrote a romance of the lost colony, issued at Charlotte in 1908. A fallen courtier looks at white trunks and a gray doublet laid for Lady Wiltshire's ball and knows he will not wear them. In four hours, he says, he passed from heaven to hell.

Raleigh, Lord North, and Francis Bacon crowd the court scene, and a viscount waits to take his place by Lady Margaret Carroll. Chapter heads promise a cave, a dice game for a life, a great armada, and a sail for Virginia. Croatan and a hunt for the lost colony close a tale of love and loss at sea.
58756-a-manual-of-pyrotechny:
A Manual of Pyrotechny, or a Familiar System of Recreative Fire-Works, was written by G W Mortimer and printed in London for W Simpkin and R Marshall in 1824. The title page carries a line of Ovid for its motto, and plates of figures open the book. Mortimer wrote because works on the subject were scarce and hard to procure.

His design is to assist readers who are fond of a rational and scientific amusement. He promises that the whole will be plain to every reader, while granting that practiced pyrotechnists may still pick up a few useful particulars. The manual belongs to the age when fireworks were a polite home science, compounded by amateurs from printed receipts rather than bought ready-made.
59957-the-shetland-pony:
The Shetland Pony is a breed history by Charles and Anne Douglas, published by William Blackwood and Sons in Edinburgh and London in 1913. An appendix on the making of the Shetland pony, by Cossar Ewart, closes the book. Gravure and other illustrations appear through the text.

The preface states the aim. The account gives, in brief outline, the chief facts of the breed's history and some idea of its present character, position, and use. The authors thought the moment right to record recent phases of its development before they were forgotten. Old spellings from writers of the 1820s and 1870s are kept in the notes. The pony's small size and hardiness suit its island home. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
60257-the-duke-of-brittany:
George Upton translated this life story for young people from the German of Henriette Jeanrenaud. McClurg published it at Chicago in 1908, with two illustrations. A plate shows Arthur's rescue of a Jew, an early scene of mercy in the tale.

Arthur, son of Geoffrey Plantagenet and Constance of Brittany, lived the brief, eventful career told here. Geoffrey was the fourth son of Henry the Second of England and Eleanor of Guienne. On the death of an elder brother, Richard the Lion-hearted became heir and took the throne in 1189. Arthur's claim, and his uncle John's grip on power, drive the story.
60692-the-history-of-the-standard-oil-co:
The History of the Standard Oil Company, by Ida Tarbell, is the famed exposure of the great oil trust, published in 1904. Volume one opens with a portrait of John Davison Rockefeller. Tarbell had already written lives of Lincoln and Napoleon. Her oil history grew from magazine work and made her name as a muckraker.

The first chapter tells the birth of the oil industry, from petroleum as a curiosity and medicine to a flood of production. Storage, transport, refining, and marketing problems follow in quick order. Later chapters reach rebates and railway favour shown to large shippers. The secret South Improvement Company scheme let Rockefeller's group force Cleveland refiners to join or sell. Tarbell wrote with care and documents at hand. Her book remains a landmark of reporting that took on the richest firm of its age.
62308-the-oak-and-the-briony:
Dean and Son of London sold a tiny tale for children in their Illustrated Farthing Books. A proud oak rears his head above his brethren of the forest, and all admire him. Age and praise have made him haughty, and he has few friends. At his root, in a quiet home of moss, a small green shoot is born.

Spring and summer feed the shoot till it grows a sound plant. Then the oak spies it and asks in scorn who dares dwell so near his noble trunk. The briony answers with meek words, saying nature chose the spot and begging leave to live. Soft speech melts the oak's anger. He bids her live in safety, and the two grow into friends, to the surprise of the whole wood. The tale teaches that pride shuts out love, while a lowly heart can win it.
62364-the-origin-of-tyranny:
The Origin of Tyranny, by P N Ure of Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge, was printed at the University Press in 1922. Ure taught classics at Reading, and his heads run the Greek world city by city. Athens comes first after the opening survey, then Samos, Egypt, and Lydia. Argos and Corinth get full turns of their own. Rome stands late in the book, a late heir of the form.

A wide ninth head sweeps Sicyon, Megara, Miletus, Ephesus, and towns of Sicily and Italy. The last study takes the rich despots of Aristotle's age, when coin bought crowns. Plates show coins, pots, and the roads of Attica from the author's own snaps. History fans get a cool, deep hunt for how one-man rule was born in the old world.
6303-the-duel-between-france-and-germany:
Charles Sumner, speaking in Boston's Music Hall on October 26, 1870, calls the war then raging between France and Germany a duel, and draws its lesson for civilization. He takes classical warrant for the word, citing Livy on affairs settled by a pure and pious duel. Dryden's line adds that when kings make war, fortune is judge and soldiers are lawyers. The lecture asks what such a duel proves about nations.

Sumner traces the Spanish throne question, family ties binding an emperor's kinsman to France, and a French cabinet that chose its own ground for defiance. He argues that France was ready, and that readiness itself shaped the quarrel. This short lecture, reprinted from addresses on war, is a plea to judge war by reason and law, not by the field alone.
63675-mutiny:
Mutiny, a science fiction story by Larry Offenbecker, was printed in Planet Stories in the fall of 1945. This mercy rocket was Rawson's first command, its headnote says, and his last, it seemed. Mutineers had taken over, then lost the ship in a quicksand pool. Captain Todd Rawson snaps angry eyes at his directional needle: the Star Flight holds her course like a bullet, though he ordered otherwise.

A call leaps in from Saturn control. Rawson answers richly: they run into a spatial storm and must detour, and will be late. For God's sake, hurry, the voice begs: the plague is wiping out the whole colony. We'll get the serum there, Rawson swears, and cuts the call with force. Old Durk, twenty years his senior, growls that the old man would have headed right into the storm. Offenbecker builds a tale of youth, mutiny, and a race against plague.
63765-mutiny:
John Perowne, rector of a Norwich church, wrote a pamphlet in 1853 on the duty to keep the Sabbath holy for all time. He wrote in reply to C J Vaughan, head master of Harrow School, whose piece dealt with whether the Crystal Palace should open on Sundays. The pamphlet sold for one shilling in London and Norwich.

Perowne says in his preface that he put the pages out with great reluctance and no love of print fights. He had hoped a man with more time and skill would answer Vaughan, whose views had, he says, already led folk to break the Sabbath. His chief aim is to set out what he holds to be Gods will on the day.
63930-the-crowded-colony:
The Crowded Colony is a tale of Mars by Jay B. Drexel, first put out in a pulp sheet of such tales in the fall of nineteen fifty. Its first lines mock the men who took the red world. Oh, how worn out these Mars folk were, those men laugh, at the dust shrines and crude small shrines in the waste. More soft laugh the Mars folk, who dream of the last laugh of all.

The tale opens in a town of Mars built when its great ditch held green, cool flow from the north ice cap. Now there is no flow, and the town clings to the high swell of the bank. Its homes step down the slope like sad brows past a dead wall baked cross and cross by the sun.
63954-mostly-about-nibble-the-bunny:
John Breck told a set of dusk tales for the young, printed at Garden City, New York in 1923 with drawings by William Andrews. Eight bunny books stand in the set's list at the front. Cheer up, Bunny, chirps Bobby Robin in the first picture. Nine short chapters fill the book.

A very small bunny has a very big adventure to open. Nibble Rabbit learns his fortune, then runs to a rescue. Lost tempers, a storm party, and a meeting with a small boy follow. Why the cow got her horns takes one chapter. Nibble fools Ouphe in his own haystack and digs into trouble, then slips out. The tale opens in rain at the mouth of the burrow.
64405-lady-maclairn-the-victim-of-villan:
Lady Maclairn, The Victim of Villany is a novel in four volumes by Mrs Hunter of Norwich, author of Letitia and The History of the Gruethorpe Family. Volume 1 was printed in London in 1806. The introduction presents the story chiefly through letters written by a Miss Cowley to her friend.

Mrs Hunter calls herself editor rather than author, saying she preferred Miss Cowley's pen to her own. The first chapter supplies the family background: Cowley, the heroine's father, was orphaned young with an ample inheritance in Jamaica, his birthplace, and placed under a London guardian deep in commerce. Novels told in letters, promising a lesson of morality along with curiosity, were a staple of the circulating libraries that this edition's many sellers supplied.
65351-the-story-of-the-indian-mutiny:
Ascott Hope wrote this history, The Story of the Indian Mutiny, printed in London and New York in 1896 with maps and pictures. Hope also wrote Men of the Backwoods. A frontispiece shows the interior of the well at Cawnpore. Nine chapters carry the rising from its outbreak to its extinction, with an appendix.

The outbreak, the spread of revolt, and the general conflagration come first. Cities of refuge follow, then the fall of Delhi and the defence of Lucknow, and Lord Clyde's campaigns. Chapter one sets the scene wide. India is a troubled land, shaped like Italy in Asia. It holds near three hundred million people. Wave after wave of conquerors wore it down, before a company of British merchants took it and held it by the sword.
65425-the-tale-of-the-great-mutiny:
The Tale of the Great Mutiny is a popular history by William Fitchett. Smith, Elder issued the third impression in London in 1903. Fitchett had earlier written Deeds That Won the Empire. Portraits and maps support the narrative. The subject is the Indian Mutiny of 1857.

The chapters move from city to city. Delhi and Cawnpore dominate the early pages. Lucknow fills three chapters in a row. The first chapter opens at Barrackpore in March 1857. A sepoy named Mungul Pandy struts before his regiment. He is drunk with bhang and with fanaticism. He shouts that biting the cartridges will ruin them all. Fitchett tells the rising as a tale of sieges and rescues.
65568-the-runaway-bunny:
