The Runaway Bunny is a children's story book by Laura Rountree Smith, printed at Chicago by the Flanagan Company in 1923. The pictures are by Dorothy Dulin. Smith wrote many books for the young: the Cotton-Tail tales, Little Bear, Little Eskimo and Seventeen Little Bears are named at the front. Ten chapters make up this book, each with its own season or feast.

The first chapter is Time to Run Away. He packs his little brown travelling bag full. A rhyme at the head begs him to form the habit of staying a while instead. Then come The County Fair, The Bunny School, The Tell-the-Time Rabbit, The Thanksgiving Dinner and Christmas at Mother Bun's. The book is a set of gentle animal tales for small children, told in short words and short chapters, with pictures throughout.
6580-charter-and-supplemental-charter-of:
King Charles the Second grants, in 1670, a royal charter to Prince Rupert and his partners for trade in Hudson's Bay. The text names dukes, earls, knights, and London merchants who paid for an expedition at their own great cost. It sets out their rights, lands, and powers in the formal, full language of a royal grant.

A later supplemental charter stands beside the first, adding to or shaping the company's legal frame. Together, the two texts form the legal root of a firm that shaped the fur trade and the map of northern North America. Readers here get the charters as they were written, not a retelling, with all their old titles and terms intact.
66601-a-point-of-testimony:
Carolyn Wells wrote A Point of Testimony, a detective story built around Bert Bayliss, the funniest detective his narrator ever saw. Bayliss is nothing like Vidocq, Lecoq, or Sherlock Holmes, the opening insists, because he has wit of his own and can hardly stay serious. He takes only cases that look hard or odd, and he invents an imaginary friend, Harris, to hear his theories.

One morning the telephone by his bed wakes him before nine. His old friend Martin Hopkins is calling from Clearbrook: a murder has been committed, and Hopkins wants him on the nine-thirty train, promising to meet him at ten. Bayliss agrees at once, glad the call is not a social one. Readers get a light-toned mystery in which a cheerful, quick mind does the work that gloom does in other detective tales.
67516-object-matrimony:
Object, Matrimony, by Bower, is a further chapter in the annals of the Hall of Mirth, as related by Bud Preston, cowboy. The narrator opens with a maxim: women are all right, if you keep far enough away from them. Trouble begins, he says, when you widen your loop for one.

The lesson came one winter on the ranch of Shooting-star Wilson. Wilson had come into ten thousand dollars from the old country, and spent every cent on a house, built to give a Washington's Birthday ball in. The cowboys called the mansion the Hall of Mirth. Its floors were painted with red, white, and blue diamonds, its ceilings with stars and stripes. The rooms were so big they echoed like thunder. Bud and Ellis would sneak down to the old bunk house for comfort. But it hurt Wilson's feelings, and besides, he wanted his money's worth of house.
6814-the-curlytops-at-uncle-frank-s-ranc:
Howard Garis sends the Curlytops, Janet and Ted Martin, to Uncle Frank's ranch, or little folks on ponyback, at Ring Rosy Ranch. Trouble's tumble opens the fun, with Ted dressed in his father's coat and hat and spectacles too large for his nose, while Janet wears her mother's things. A collision, cowboy fun, bad news, and a queer noise follow.

A sick pony, a surprised doctor, a lasso, a bucking bronco, missing cattle, and a hidden valley test the children's pluck. Garis writes with bright, simple humor for young readers. The Curlytops at Uncle Frank's Ranch is a cheerful western for small children, full of ponies and play.
68580-a-handbook-of-systematic-botany:
A Handbook of Systematic Botany, by Warming of Copenhagen, is a full text on the sorting of plants into kinds. The English text came out in London in 1895 with six hundred and ten drawings. Potter of Durham translated and edited the work.

The English book rests on the third Danish edition of 1892 and on a German edition of 1890. Knoblauch revised the fungi for this text, using the newer work of Brefeld. Other hands revised the bacteria and the red algae for the same pages. Warming sent fresh notes of his own to enrich the book. The result is a survey of the whole plant kingdom as scholars then carved it up, group by group and form by form.
69038-lot-company:
Will Levington Comfort wrote Lot and Company, copyrighted in New York in 1915. Comfort had written Red Fleece, Midstream, and Down Among Men. He gives the novel to Jane. Contents fall in seven parts, under three heads that return. The Jade opens and comes back in part three. Lot and Company stands in parts two and six. The open boat fills part four, and the stone house parts five and seven.

The first part opens on a Sunday afternoon in a boarding-house. All would have happened otherwise for Bellair, the text says, had he been drowsy as usual. A smell of carpets drives him forth into a November day of gusts, wisps of sunshine, and threats of rain. He walks east, crosses to Brooklyn, and follows the water-front. At a wooden arch marked Hatmos and Company, he finds a sailing-ship putting forth, the Jade of Adelaide.
69193-children-of-destiny:
Children of Destiny is a novel by Molly Elliot Seawell, illustrated by Wenzell and published in New York by Burt. Copyrights of 1893 and 1903 stand on the page. An illustration notes a certain quality of attraction about Blair which made women love him.

The first chapter opens in splendour. Hot June sunshine pours down on the great fields of yellow wheat at Deerchase. The velvet wind sweeps over them, making long billows and shadowy dimples in the golden sea of grain. The air is all blue and gold, alive with the music of harvest: the wind in the wheat, the droning of bees, the drumming of the cicada. Above all comes the song of the Black reapers swinging their scythes in the morning sun. Woods murmur on one side; live oaks and elms shade a spacious brick house on the other. Seawell's Virginia romance begins in a harvest idyll.
69240-a-port-said-miscellany:
A Port Said Miscellany is a sea essay by William McFee, issued as number six of the Atlantic Readings. The Atlantic Monthly Press at Boston published it with copyright of 1918. The paper had first appeared in The Atlantic Monthly for March 1918. McFee was a ship's engineer, and the essay is written from the engine room side of a troopship.

The scene is the Mediterranean in wartime. The smoke from the funnel goes straight up, and the iron bulwarks are as hot as a hand can bear. Under the awnings the troops lie gasping on their rubber sheets. The escort crosses and recrosses ahead. Then a keen eye catches a fraying of the horizon line: Port Said is in sight. The news wakes everybody, and rations are packed and rifles cleaned.
69421-the-humour-of-germany:
Müller-Casenov selected and translated this anthology of German humor for Walter Scott at London in 1892. It stands in the International Humour series, with an introduction and a biographical index, and illustrations by Brock. The range is six centuries. Hugo von Trimberg's Master Fox, from about 1300, opens it, and Hans Sachs tells St Peter's lesson. Grimmelshausen raids the parson's kitchen from the Thirty Years' War.

Tieck, Jean Paul, and Kotzebue carry the tale into the age of Goethe. Chamisso's man who sold his shadow is here in extract, and Heine gets a sheaf of pieces to himself, tourists at the Brocken among them. Hauff's night in the Bremen Rathskeller and Mörike's Mozart on his journey to Prague follow. Reuter's Low German fun and Keller's Swiss stories close the earlier masters. The volume argues, by exhibit, that Germany laughs in more dialects than one.
69537-the-holy-war-made-in-germany:
The Holy War Made in Germany is an essay by Snouck Hurgronje of Leiden, published in 1915. Hurgronje, the leading Dutch scholar of Islam, examines Germany's attempt to raise a holy war among Muslims against the Allied powers.

He begins with a Turkish thinker who remarked that men now kill over politics as bitterly as ever over religion. The sceptical irony, Hurgronje says, was justified by 1914, when every belligerent disclaimed responsibility for crimes all had prepared together. Against that background he considers what Muslim teaching on religion and war actually holds, and how far a jihad proclaimed from Berlin could command belief.
69943-the-training-of-an-infantry-compan:
Kirkpatrick wrote a field training guide for an infantry company, in a second form printed in 1914. Opening pages set out the aim of the book and how a commander can make the best of his men. Ground, dress, scouts, and the mood of the unit all count as part of sound training.

Drills then work through attack, retreat, and fire control for small groups in the field. Sections and platoons learn to advance, hold, and fall back in good order. Later parts cover camps, marches, guards, and field works, so a young officer can plan each day of training with care.
70031-the-women-of-the-mayflower-and-wom:
Ethel Noyes honors the mothers of a colony in The Women of the Mayflower and Women of Plymouth Colony. The book was printed at Plymouth, Massachusetts, in 1921 by the Memorial Press. Noyes holds the copyright, and a foreword fronts her text.

The foreword owns the gap she fills. The Pilgrim women have been writ of so little, it says. History has dwelt long on the Pilgrim Fathers and their great venture. It passed the women by with a broad word and now and then a tribute. These women loved liberty and bore hardship for its sake. They built the homes of the nation and raised their kin in stern virtues and a living faith.
70490-polite-bunny:
Laura Rountree Smith wrote and Penny Ross drew a children's manners book copyrighted at Chicago in 1922. Pretty Bunny Manners lives with Old Father and Mother Bun in a little house in the woods. Chapter one brings a letter from Aunt Etiquette. Pretty Bunny warns her brother Healthy Bunny that she will always call good morning.

Healthy Bunny often forgets, so she makes up a good morning song. It is sung to the tune of Twinkle Little Star. Chapters then teach bedroom manners, table manners, and school manners. Shopping and street manners follow, with tales about being on time and picking things up. Company manners close the lessons. Color pictures show ice cream and cake.
70872-spears-of-destiny:
Howden Smith wrote this story of the first capture of Constantinople, copyrighted by Doran in 1919. Smith dedicates the book to Hoffman in a spirit somewhat malicious, the dedication jokes. In Crowden Wood opens the contents, and strangers at Blancherive follow in the greenwood.

A knife in the twilight, a jongleur and the greenwood men fill the early chapters. Hugh gains a friend, meets a swart shipman and faces sea-wolves in the list. The comrades take the cross, Venice's doge bargains and the imperial city falls, in a tale of the Fourth Crusade told as high adventure.
70909-pan-germany:
Pan Germany, The Disease and Cure is a war tract by Andre Cheradame. A New Hampshire defence league spread the book in America during the war. Governor Keyes headed the league list as honorary president of the branch. A Concord letter dated February first nineteen eighteen states the league purpose.

The league wished to bring knowledge of the German plan to New Hampshire folk. Cheradame, a French writer, laid out the Pan German scheme for world sway. His cure turns on Allied victory and a firm peace settlement after. Lists of league officers from across the state front this American edition. The book belongs to the home front print war of nineteen seventeen.
71165-lady-maclairn-the-victim-of-villan:
Mrs Hunter of Norwich wrote this novel in four volumes, of which this is the second. Earle and Hucklebridge printed Lady Maclairn, the Victim of Villany, at London in 1806. Hunter had earlier written Letitia and The History of the Grubthorpe Family.

The tale runs in letters, in the manner of the day. Letter thirteen opens this volume, from Miss Cowley to Miss Hardcastle. Cowley warns that her friend will plead Rachel Cowley's health as a plea to leave Tarefield. Facts are stubborn things, she answers: Rachel bore the trial with no fever on her nerves. A cold gave her a thin plea to stay in, and the plot of ill use turns on such small hinges.
71396-lady-maclairn-the-victim-of-villan:
Lady Maclairn, the Victim of Villany, a novel in four volumes by Hunter of Norwich, reaches its third volume in a London printing of 1806. Hunter also wrote Letitia, The Unexpected Legacy, and The History of the Grubthorpe Family. Chapter one warns that the reader must again be content with the narrator's pen, to supply the interrupted course of Cowley's letters.

From the period already described, the lovers were left to their own discretion and the direction of Counsellor Steadman. Steadman, using Sinclair's information, supported their attachment. The heroine gives her lover to understand that she means not to marry till Flamall's power has ceased. She will be mistress of herself and her fortune, she says, and show her own judgment in choosing a man worthy of both. The tale is an epistolary novel of persecuted virtue.
72019-frankie-s-dog-tony:
Madeline Leslie, writing as Aunt Hattie, wrote this story for boys, printed in Chicago in 1880 and entered for copyright in 1867. It is volume four of Aunt Hattie's Library for Boys. Chapter one promises to tell of a dog who wore a coat and was a great traveller, a dog Frank was proud of.

Frank Colvin lives with his parents and his brother Edward in a cottage near Boston. His father, a sea captain, once brought home an English officer wounded in the war. The chapter list points ahead to Frankie's music lessons, the theft of the dog, and Tony's love for her master, before a short closing chapter.
7238-my-four-years-in-germany:
James W. Gerard, late ambassador to the German imperial court, wrote My Four Years in Germany as a warning to his own people, and he puts that warning first as a foreword. He wants readers to grasp the gravity of the situation: German military and naval power, he insists, stood unbroken, and the twelve million men under arms could not be waved away.

Illustrations of court balls, safe conducts, and a special train of Americans leaving in August 1914 frame the memoir's insider view. Gerard dedicates the book to his wife, his small but tactful family of one, and his tone mixes diplomacy with plain alarm. The memoir reads as testimony from inside Berlin on the edge of war.
73531-beginners-botany:
Bailey wrote Beginners' Botany for Macmillan, printed at Toronto in 1921. The book was allowed for use in Ontario schools by the minister of education. Its twenty-four chapters lead a young reader from first looks to full plant lore. It starts with the plain fact that no two plants or parts are quite alike. Then come the struggle to live, survival of the fit, and plant groups that live side by side.

Later parts take up roots, stems, leaves, and the work each part does. The flower, its parts and its seed-making, get close care. Fruits, seed spread, and low plants without true flowers close the book. Bailey writes in plain terms with prints to aid the eye. Young hands can use it in the field, the school plot, and at home.
73803-the-shears-of-destiny:
The Shears of Destiny is a novel of Russia by Leroy Scott. Doubleday, Page and Company published it in New York in 1910. Alexander Popini drew the illustrations. Henry Drexel, a young American business man, travels to Russia on family business. His uncle John Howard is an American capitalist. His cousin Alice is engaged to Prince Berloff.

Princess Olga Valenko and her father govern the other camp. General Valenko rules St Petersburg as military governor. Against them stand the revolutionists of the Central Committee. Their hidden leader is called the White One. Captain Nadson of the political police hunts them all. The first chapter, The Woman in Brown, shortens Drexel's Moscow business to two pleasant days. Prisoners, bargains, and a battle in Three Saints' Court drive the plot to its desperate close.
74288-two-way-destiny:
Frank Belknap Long wrote the novelette Two Way Destiny, first printed in the magazine Fantastic Universe in October 1954. The magazine's own introduction frames the tale as a study of why some peoples prize hate and war while others live at peace. Long sets that question on a lovely alien world and lets two people carry it.

The narrator, alone on the planet Dracona, comes on a girl kneeling by a stream in a forest clearing. She is not from Earth, and she is out gathering specimens: spider bats, darter birds, and a flying lizard thrashing in the net at her back. The cover line sets the pair on a lost Eden under a cloud of tribal hate. Readers get a first-person tale in which a meeting between two strangers from unlike peoples tests whether hate or trust will govern their shared world.
74355-army-boys-marching-into-germany:
Homer Randall's Army Boys Marching into Germany, or Over the Rhine with the Stars and Stripes, was copyrighted in nineteen nineteen by George Sully and Company of New York. It is the fifth volume of his Army Boys series for boys, after training camp, the French trenches, the firing line, and the big drive. A front plate shows two forces meeting with a tremendous shock.

The contents race through the war's end. A disguised officer, a trap, a tunnel fight, and Colonel Pavet's return lead to tank against tank and liquid fire. Then come the white flag of surrender, victory, the Rhine crossing, and a German plot foiled in a cellar. The first chapter opens mid-sentence on a shouted order to hold the position.
7465-richard-of-jamestown-a-story-of-the:
James Otis wrote this story to show children the home life of the colonists they meet in history books. His hero is Richard Mutton, whose name stands in the list of those sent to Virginia by the London Company on December 19, 1606. The story is told from a child's viewpoint, as if related by a child, so young readers meet Jamestown at their own eye level.

Otis deliberately avoids romance, dealing only with facts so far as possible. He describes daily life: the voyage, the settlement, and the hard work of conquering a wilderness for conscience or for gain. The book belongs to a series on colonial home life, and it still serves its purpose well: history as lived experience, not as a list of dates.
74696-wind-of-destiny:
Sara Lindsay Coleman wrote a novel dated 1916, in a form first capped at a small run of fine copies. The tale runs in letters, the first from a young nurse in a New York hospital to her friend Caroline. Dicky, once Henrietta Dickenson, has replied to a lone hearts note in the Herald, to the shock of her kin.

Probes in the ward must paste flat to the wall when their betters pass, and may not speak to the young doctors. One night walk past lit doors on the Avenue wakes in Dicky a fierce wish for one taste of city night. Calm town life and wild town life clash through the two friends words.
7499-through-five-republics-on-horseback:
G. Whitfield Ray, pioneer missionary and government explorer, rode through South America on horseback, and this book, in a revised twelfth edition of 1915, tells of those wanderings. The Reverend J. G. Brown of the Canadian Baptist missions introduces it. Ray's own preface quotes the Missionary Review of the World, which had called South America the darkest land, and claims that he penetrated part of its unexplored country.

The wanderings cross five republics, through regions where few outsiders had been. Ray writes as both missionary and explorer, noting peoples, rivers, and trails with a traveler's eye. An earlier editor, the book notes, abused it while admitting it sold like hot cakes. Readers bought it anyway, and had their eyes opened, as Ray intended.
76038-pyrotechny:
Pyrotechny is a handbook of firework making issued by Ward, Lock, and Tyler of London. Its full title promises the art of making fireworks at little cost, and with complete safety and cleanliness. One hundred and twenty-four illustrations of forms and diagrams support the text.

General requisites come first: scales and weights, pestle and mortar, and sieves. Rockets fill the longest section. Cases are rolled, choked, rammed, and primed by rule. Stars are made in brilliant, tailed, and coloured kinds, with golden rain to finish. Roman candles, gerbes, and jets follow. Wheels turn horizontally and vertically by several devices. Lances and coloured lights serve for set-pieces and illuminations. Tourbillons, Bengal fires, and Chinese flyers come next. Mines of serpents and crackers and a five-pointed star close the teaching. Exhibition pieces end the book.
76172-a-bad-penny:
A Bad Penny, a novel by John Wheelwright, was first copyrighted in 1896 and reissued in Boston in 1901 with drawings by Attwood. Wheelwright was known for A Child of the Century and Rollo's Journey to Cambridge. The tale is set in Oldbury, a quiet New England seaport town that trade has left behind.

The opening paints a great square brick house on broad High Street, built by a Yankee ship owner, with elms, a white-pillared porch, and a wide lawn. Plate titles name Deacon Fairbanks, Alice, and Cheever, and hint at boat chases, bold looks, and old wrongs. The story mixes town gossip, youth, and money trouble in a slow, observant way.
77438-the-black-company:
W B M Ferguson deals a chess-flavored mystery in The Black Company, from Chelsea House of New York, copyrighted in 1924. The narrator tells it in the first person, chapter by chapter: I Take a Ride, I Find a Job, I Hear Some News. One chapter is titled King's Pawn to Knight's, and a later one I Find Myself a Murderer.

The Black King, an interview with His Majesty, and I Win the Queen close the game. The tale opens at the Princeton Inn after the last nip-and-tuck baseball game with Yale, in a private room where everyone but Pete, the narrator, is far from sober.
77839-the-countess-fanny:
Marjorie Bowen wrote this Cornish sea piece, set in 1856 and published by Hodder and Stoughton. A prologue opens with the one man who might know the truth of the story. He was the one man who could never speak that truth, the prologue says at the start.

In old age, with passions stilled, he spoke of the Contessina Francesca Caldini, called Fanny. Her grandson asks whether she could really have been there and then got away, the prologue goes on. It was a madman's suggestion, the old man answers smiling, and a woman's reputation hangs on the silence that Bowen's tale slowly breaks.
78430-a-practical-course-in-botany:
Andrews's A Practical Course in Botany, revised by Francis Lloyd of McGill University and issued by the American Book Company in 1911, teaches plant study with reference to farming, business and health. Andrews had already written Botany All the Year Round.

The course climbs the plant in order: the seed and its stored food, germination and growth, the root and osmosis, the stem and its work. Buds and branches and the leaf follow, each chapter ending in field work. Full-page plates show live oaks near Savannah, water carried over the Mississippi levee by siphon to rice fields, a Mexican strangling fig's aerial roots, and gooseberries improved by selection.
78733-the-master-of-destiny:
The Master of Destiny: A Biography of the Brain, by Frederick Tilney, was printed by Doubleday, Doran at Garden City in 1930, with first words by Austen Fox Riggs. Tilney also wrote The Brain from Ape to Man. He starts as any good life tale should: at the start. If man sprang from a lone act of making, so did his brain; if he rose by slow change, the brain rose with him. The sciences, he says, back the slow road.

Heads climb the scale: first beasts with no true brain, the brain from fish to man, and man in the making. Eden meets Darwin in one head. Gibbon, orang, chimp, and gorilla take their turns, then cave man at last. Hand, foot, and brain share credit for man's rise. Brain fans get a full life of the mind's house.
79317-sonny:
Murray Leinster, a prolific pen of the pulp years, wrote this western under the title Sonny. Its hero, Sonny Holman, rides into the town of Helada worth a thousand dollars to anyone who takes him, dead or alive. He does not yet know that the alarm has gone out for him.

In the livery corral a black and white horse named Gunpowder is throwing every rider. Sonny watches the brute buck a man off, then ropes it as it rears over the fallen rider. The head note says Sonny needs just such a fierce mount for a long search ahead. To pay for the horse, he takes on a risky task for the sheriff of Helada.
79365-in-a-german-colony:
In a German Colony, or Four Weeks in New Britain, by Pullen-Burry, was first published at London by Methuen in 1909. The author had written Jamaica As It Is and Ethiopia in Exile. Eight pictures and two maps go with the text. A woman from the bush villages fronts the book.

The first chapter tells of the voyage out on the Prinz Waldemar. An incident in the German consulate at Sydney opens the account. The Maoris and their present state get early notice. The second chapter takes up the confusing names of the protectorate. Papuan and Melanesian types are set side by side. Blanche Bay, Simpsonhafen, and a walk to Matupi ground the tour. The book reports a German Pacific colony for British readers.
8880-satanstoe-or-the-littlepage-manuscr:
James Fenimore Cooper writes Satanstoe, or the Littlepage Manuscripts. A tale of the colony, opening with Spenser's line that the only amaranthine flower on earth is virtue, and the only treasure, truth. His preface argues that every chronicle of manners has value, and double value when customs connect with principles in origin, development, or end. The Littlepage manuscripts, he says, show such a connection with important theories of Cooper's own time.

The novel follows the Littlepage family in colonial New York, through land, society, and the tensions that would become the anti-rent wars. Cooper, writing late in his career, uses a family chronicle to defend landed order and to criticize democratic excess as he saw it. Readers of American historical fiction will find a rich, if partisan, portrait of colonial life, and the first volume of a trilogy that runs into the early republic.
903-the-white-company:
Arthur Conan Doyle wrote this romance of the Hundred Years' War, about Alleyne Edricson, a young man who leaves his abbey. He joins the White Company, a band of English archers in France. Sir Nigel Loring leads them, and Samkin Aylward, the bowman, becomes Alleyne's friend and guide.

Doyle fills the tale with castles, battles, and chivalry, from the Pied Merlin inn to the fields of Spain. Alleyne grows from cloistered youth to tested man, learning honour, love, and war. The novel is a stirring, old-fashioned adventure, and a showcase for Doyle beyond Sherlock Holmes, rich in medieval colour.
a-century-too-soon-the-age-of-tyranny: John Roy Musick sets this romance a century too soon, in the age of tyranny after the Restoration in England. Historians, he notes, had paid little attention to that period in the American colonies, a hundred years before liberty was won. The story follows colonists whose hopes stir as the sleeping goddess of liberty seems to wake. Musick blends adventure and history in a tale of early resistance.
a-ryght-profytable-treatyse-compendiousl: Thomas Betson gathers writings of holy men into this short devotional treatise, printed at Caxton's house by Wynkyn de Worde around 1500. The tract was reprinted at Cambridge in 1905. It was one of twenty-six bound together in a volume given to the University in 1715 by King George the First, with the library of John Moore, Bishop of Ely. The author's name survives only from the colophon, read as Betson against an older reading of Betton.
brandes-main-currents-5-the-romantic-sch:
German Romantic writing fills the fifth book of Brandes's Main Currents, here in English. The Schlegels, Tieck, Novalis, and Hoffmann taught Europe new ways to dream and to doubt. Poetry, philosophy, and sly irony blend in their work.

Brandes traces how a circle of young talents remade German letters in a few bold years. He treats their longing for the infinite with sympathy and sharp insight. Fragments, fairy tales, and night pieces all find their place in his account. The volume shows why Romantic ideas from Germany spread so far across the whole of Europe.
brandes-main-currents-6-young-germany:
Young Germany closes Brandes's vast survey, in this sixth and final English book. Heine, Borne, and their allies turned writing into a weapon of politics. Literature left the study and entered the street fight for a freer Germany.

Brandes gives these radical voices his warmest praise and fullest energy. Wit, verse, and prose all serve one cause: breaking the grip of kings and censors. The survey ends where the modern age of engaged writing begins. Few works of criticism match the sweep of the full six books or their lasting sway over readers in many lands.
britannica-1911-abergavenny:
Abergavenny receives a town entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, inside a shared chunk of text. The Monmouthshire market town stands where the Gavenny joins the Usk, ringed by high hills, with 7,795 folk in 1901. Roman Gobannium guarded the Usk road on the same ground.

St Mary's church, once a Benedictine priory's, holds memorials from the thirteenth to seventeenth centuries. Castle remains recall border war: Welsh seizure in 1175, Charles the First judging parliamentarians in 1645. Charters rose and fell, one annulled in 1688 when officers refused William's oath. Welsh flannel and goats'-hair periwigs were old town trades. The Neville barony of Abergavenny, from Edward Neville's summons in 1450, rose to an earldom in 1784 and a marquessate in 1876.
britannica-1911-agrimony:
Agrimony, an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica, describes a slender perennial herb found across the north temperate zone. Its botanical name is Agrimonia Eupatoria, and it belongs to the rose family, Rosaceae. The plant grows one to three feet high in hedge-banks, copses, and field borders. Its leafy stem ends in spikes of small yellow flowers.

Once flowering ends, the stalk bends back and the fruit carries many small hooks. Those hooks catch on rough objects, such as an animal's coat, and so spread the seed. The underground woody stem is astringent, meaning it tightens tissue, and yields a yellow dye. Several unrelated plants sharing the agrimony name, from hemp agrimony to water agrimony, are listed at the end.
britannica-1911-albert-iii-duke-of-saxon:
Albert III, duke of Saxony, surnamed Animosus, the Courageous, who lived from 1443 to 1500, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Younger son of Frederick II, the Mild, he was born in January 1443. As a boy he was kidnapped with his brother Ernest by Kunz von Kaufungen and escaped. He spent time afterwards at the emperor Frederick III's court in Vienna.

In 1464 Albert married Sidonia, daughter of George Podebrad of Bohemia, though the Bohemian crown escaped him later. Ruling jointly with Ernest after their father's death, he took Meissen at the division of Leipzig in 1485 and founded the Albertine branch of the Wettin family. The emperor valued him as a soldier against Charles the Bold and Matthias Corvinus. Maximilian made him hereditary governor of Friesland in 1498, a title he still had to fight to make good.
britannica-1911-albert-king-of-saxony:
Albert, Frederick Augustus, king of Saxony, who lived from 1828 to 1902, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in April 1828, he was the eldest son of Prince John, who later took the throne. His education was largely military, as befitted a German prince, though he also attended lectures at Bonn. His first warfare came in 1849 against the Danes in Schleswig-Holstein.

As crown-prince in 1866 he commanded the Saxon forces against Prussia. Falling back into Bohemia, the Saxons joined the Austrians, fought on the Iser line and at Gitchin, and held the extreme left at Koniggratz with great tenacity. Their retreat stayed in good order despite defeat. In the war with France he received a separate command, the army of the Meuse, made up of Saxons, the Prussian Guard, and a Prussian corps, for the march toward Paris.
britannica-1911-alimony:
Alimony, a legal allowance, is explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. From the Latin alere, to nourish, alimony is the maintenance a wife is entitled to claim from her husband's estate. It applies when a court decrees judicial separation or dissolves the marriage. As a rule it is payable to a wife, though circumstances can make a wife pay it to a husband.

Two kinds are distinguished. Temporary alimony, granted pending the suit, lets the wife live while the case proceeds, and it is allowed whoever brought the suit. English practice allotted about one fifth of the husband's net income, though a husband without means, or a wife earning her own living, changes the calculation. Permanent alimony follows the final decree. A summary kind gives a deserted or cruelly treated wife a weekly sum, capped at two pounds, under the act of 1895. American state practice is compared at the end.
britannica-1911-allegheny:
Allegheny was a city of Allegheny county, Pennsylvania, standing on the north bank of the Allegheny and Ohio rivers opposite Pittsburgh. Since 1907 it has formed part of Pittsburgh itself. Its population reached 129,896 in 1900, with large German, Irish, and Austrian communities among the foreign-born. Railways on many lines and Ohio river boats served the city.

Riverfront manufactories and shipping headquarters ran for miles along the banks, while residence districts climbed the hills behind the business quarter. The entry lists a city park, Riverview Park with its astronomical observatory, a theological seminary, and other institutions. A long closing section recounts the contested annexation: voters in every ward opposed it, yet state and federal supreme courts upheld the act in 1907.
britannica-1911-anne-of-brittany:
Anne of Brittany was the daughter of the duke of Brittany and his wife, and came to the duchy as a girl of not yet twelve on her fathers death. At once her hand and her lands drew a ring of hunters. The king of France sought sway over her, a great lord sought to wed her, and a rival claimed her duchy.

Her own guardian rose in revolt against his lord, the 1911 Britannica entry says. A French host marched into Brittany the next year. To guard her free rule she made a pact with a prince of Austria and wed him by proxy. He could not shield her, and in the end she was forced to treat with the French king and wed him in place of her first lord. Terms were struck for the rights of each to the crown of her land.
britannica-1911-antimony:
Antimony is a metal like element grouped with nitrogen, phosphorus, arsenic, and bismuth. A 1911 Britannica entry traces its use back to very early times in the East. Its sulphide was known as kohl and named in the Old Testament. Greek and Latin writers used forms of the word stibium for the same stuff.

Native metal antimony is rare and was first clearly known as such in 1748. It occurs in thin plates or grainy masses with a tin white gleam. The entry notes it is found in limestone and in veins with silver ores. Basil Valentine wrote of it near 1600 and told how to prepare the metal.
britannica-1911-autogeny:
Autogeny means self-production, or spontaneous generation. The Greek root word means self-made. Haeckel split the idea in two. He used autogeny when the fluid in which first life was thought to arise held no carbon-based matter. He used plasmogeny when that fluid was of the organic kind. In that case the fluid held the needed base stuffs in complex, fluid mixes of carbon.

The word has a quite separate use in metal work. In autogenous soldering, two pieces of metal are joined with no solder at all. The faces that meet are melted. They fuse to each other as they cool. No third metal serves as a cement. So one short piece joins a term from the science of life to a term from the workshop. Each use rests on the same thought: the thing acts, or is made, from itself.
britannica-1911-babington-anthony:
Babington, Anthony is a life article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an English conspirator. Born in October 1561, the son of Henry Babington of Dethick in Derbyshire, he was raised in secret as a Roman Catholic. As a youth he served at Sheffield as page to Mary queen of Scots. In 1580 he came to London and joined the society backing the Jesuit missionaries.

The article tells the plot that destroyed him. In April 1586 Babington led a plan to murder Elizabeth, raise a Catholic revolt and free Mary. His open folly undid it: hungry for Mary's thanks, he wrote her long letters, which Walsingham's spies intercepted. Ballard was seized in August and betrayed the rest. Babington fled, was caught late in August, and was condemned for high treason.
britannica-1911-baden-germany:
Baden, or Baden-Baden, is a German town and fashionable watering-place in the grand-duchy of Baden, set on a hill in a beautiful Black Forest valley south of Karlsruhe. Its pleasure grounds, gardens, and brilliant season life draw crowds from all the world, over 70,000 visitors a year against some 16,000 residents.

Twenty-nine hot springs pour from the castle rock at ninety gallons a minute, piped through town to two bathing houses counted Europe's most elegant. The waters are held specific for chronic rheumatism, gout, paralysis, and neuralgia, among other ills. A conversation house, pump-room, theatre, and gallery serve the season, though the famous public gaming tables were abolished. Romans knew the springs, and tradition credits Hadrian with founding the town.
britannica-1911-balcony:
Balcony is the name for a platform that juts out from the wall of a building. The word comes through Italian from a term for a scaffold or beam. Such a platform rests on columns or brackets and is fenced by a balustrade, a low rail of small posts.

The 1911 Britannica entry gives special uses as well. At St Peter's in Rome, a balcony serves the new pope when he gives his blessing to the city and the world. Churches may hold singers in a balcony, halls may hold musicians, and in theatres the word names the seats above the dress circle.
britannica-1911-barony:
Barony is, first, the domain of a baron. Beyond that core sense, the word does different work in the three kingdoms, and the 1911 Britannica entry sorts the uses one by one. In Ireland, counties are divided into baronies, which match the hundreds of England.

Those Irish baronies seem to have been formed from the territories of the Irish chiefs, as each chief submitted to English rule. In Scotland, the term applies to any large freehold estate, even when a commoner holds it. Barony also denotes the rank or dignity of a baron himself, and the feudal tenure called tenure by barony, the holding of land by that rank's service.
britannica-1911-bek-antony:
Antony Bek (died 1311) was bishop of Durham under Edward I. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica traces his rise from a Lincolnshire family in the church. Royal favor won him the Durham see in 1283 by election. Edward used him in Scottish affairs and on a mission to Germany.

He took the surrender of John de Baliol at Brechin in 1296. At Falkirk in 1298 he led a division of the English army. A fierce feud with his own prior brought royal anger on him. The king seized his lands for a time in that quarrel. Wealth, pride, and a soldier bent mark the portrait throughout.
britannica-1911-cassel-germany:
Cassel is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a German city on the river Fulda, capital of the old electorate of Hesse-Cassel. Since Prussia took it in 1866 it has headed the province of Hesse-Nassau. Its people rose from 64,083 in 1885 to 120,446 in 1905. The city stands in hilly, well wooded country 124 miles by rail from Frankfort, and a stone bridge joins its parts across the Fulda. Narrow crooked streets and gabled houses fill the old town, while the new towns and suburbs rank among the finest in Germany.

The great square Friedrichs-platz fronts the old electoral palace and the Museum Fridericianum, which holds mosaics, coins, casts, and a library of 230,000 volumes. The picture gallery holds one of the finest small collections in Europe, rich in Rembrandt, Frans Hals, and Van Dyck.
britannica-1911-chalcedony:
Chalcedony is a mineral article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a kind of silica often used as an ornamental stone. The modern use of the term is fairly new. The chalcedonius of Pliny was a quite different stone, a green one from the copper mines of Chalcedon in Asia Minor. That town gave the name.

Old writers also muddled it with a red stone from Africa shipped through Carthage. Our chalcedony was most likely classed by the ancients among the jaspers and agates. Modern mineral men limit the name to forms of silica that do not grow as distinct crystals like quartz. They grow in rounded, lumpy, or hanging forms and break with a fine splintery break. A delicate fibrous structure shows inside. In short, chalcedony is quartz built of crystals too small to see.
britannica-1911-chaumont-en-bassigny:
Chaumont-en-Bassigny is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of eastern France, capital of the department of Haute Marne. It stands 163 miles east south east of Paris on the main Eastern railway line to Belfort. Its population in 1906 was 12,089. The town sits on a height between the Marne and the Suize, near their meeting. A lofty viaduct over the Suize carries the railway to the west.

The church of St Jean Baptiste dates from the thirteenth century, with later choir and chapels. Its sculptured triforium and a Holy Sepulchre reward a look inside. The Tour Hautefeuille, an eleventh century keep, is the chief relic of a château of the counts of Champagne. Glove making and leather dressing are the main industries. In 1814 the town hosted the treaty by which Britain, Austria, Russia, and Prussia bound themselves to make no separate peace with Napoleon.
britannica-1911-chauny:
Chauny is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of northern France, in the department of Aisne. It stands 19 miles south by west of St Quentin by rail. Its population in 1906 was 10,127. The town sits on the Oise, where the river becomes navigable. The canal of St Quentin meets the lateral canal of the Oise there. That junction gives the town an active trade.

Its works include mirror polishing shops tied to the mirror works of St Gobain. Chemical works, sugar factories, metal foundries, and breweries also operate. The entry adds one line of history. Chauny was the scene of much fighting in the Hundred Years' War. The whole account is brief: place, water, trade, works, and wars. It gives a compact profile of a canal town whose business rested on the river and the glass trade of its neighbour.
britannica-1911-chauvigny:
Chauvigny is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of western France, in the department of Vienne. It stands 20 miles east of Poitiers by rail. Its population in 1906 was 2326. The town is finely set above the Vienne and a small torrent. It has two interesting Romanesque churches, both restored in modern times. Ruins of a château of the bishops of Poitiers also survive, with those of other strongholds.

Near the town lies the curious bone cavern of Jioux. Large blocks of stone fortify its entrance. Lime burning and plaster making are the local trades. Stone quarries work in the neighbourhood. Trade is in wool and feathers. The short entry gives a small town in a strong river site, marked by its churches, its ruined castles, and its odd cavern. Nothing is added beyond what those features and trades supply.
britannica-1911-collins-anthony:
Anthony Collins (1676–1729) was an English deist born at Heston, near Hounslow, on 21 June 1676. He studied at Eton and at King's College, Cambridge. For a time he read law at the Middle Temple. The high point of his life, the entry holds, was his close friendship with Locke. Locke's letters speak of him with warm praise.

In 1715 he settled in Essex and held local office there. He died in Harley Street, London, on 13 December 1729. His books gather the yield of earlier English free thought. Calm courtesy marks his style, in sharp contrast to the rage of his foes. The entry is firm on one point. Collins was no atheist, and not even an agnostic by his own account. He held that ignorance founds atheism and free thought cures it.
britannica-1911-colony:
A colony, in the common sense, is a settlement of a state's subjects in lands beyond its bounds. Such settlers owe loyalty to no foreign power. They keep a greater or lesser tie of dependence on the mother country. The word comes from the Latin colonia, from a term for a cultivator. Founding and ruling such places fills a long page of history.

Trade drove the first great wave. The Phoenicians planted colonies on islands and along the south shore of the Mediterranean from love of commerce. They left marks of sea power past the Pillars of Hercules. Carthage, their chief offshoot, planted colonies of her own. Hers served war, to guard gains and add strength. Those child colonies stayed in strict bond to her. The entry then moves to Greek and Roman practice. Roman colonies spread the rudiments of Roman life through the provinces.
britannica-1911-company:
Company is a word for a group of folk joined for a shared aim, explains a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Its root points to eating bread together, the entry says. Like words are partnership, union, gild, and corporation, each with its own shade of sense.

In British use the word is now held by two great classes. First are joint stock companies, formed under a law of nineteen oh eight. That law drew together acts from eighteen sixty two onward. Second are public companies, formed by a special act for works of public use. Railways, docks, gas works, and water works are cases. A joint stock company is defined in full, as folk who join funds to run a trade venture.
britannica-1911-felony:
Felony is a law article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a class of grave offences in English law. The word comes from Old French, and its deep root is obscure. It may tie to the Latin for gall, or to a verb meaning to deceive. Coke read it as a crime done with a heart full of gall.

Other writers tied it to fee, a fief or land held of a lord. On that view a felony was an act for which a man lost his fee. Acts that brought forfeiture were called felonies in feudal law, though some had no criminal cast at all. A vassal's breach of duty counted: neglect of service, or delay in seeking his lord's grant, was felony.
britannica-1911-flavigny:
Flavigny is a town of eastern France, in the department of Cote-d'Or. It stands on a promontory above the river Ozerain, 33 miles west-north-west of Dijon by road. Its population in 1906 was only 725. Among its antiquities are remains of an eighth-century abbey. That abbey is now a factory making anise, an industry tied to the town since the seventeenth century. Its church, of the thirteenth and fifteenth centuries, holds carved stalls and a fine rood-screen.

A Dominican convent, old houses and ancient gateways add to the town's interest. About three miles north-west rises Mont Auxois, the probable site of ancient Alesia. There Caesar defeated the Gallic chief Vercingetorix, whose statue now crowns the hill. Many Gallo-Roman remains have been dug from its slopes. The short entry thus links a small anise-making town with one of the famous battlefields of Roman Gaul.
britannica-1911-frederick-i-elector-of-s:
Frederick I (1369-1428), called the Warlike, elector and duke of Saxony, was born at Altenburg on 29 March 1369, eldest son of Frederick the Stern of the house of Wettin. After family divisions he ruled Meissen and Thuringia with his brothers, becoming sole ruler in 1425. He fought for the Teutonic Order in 1391 and backed Rupert III against King Wenceslaus.

The Hussite danger bound him to King Sigismund, and he led in the early war against them at great cost. Sigismund rewarded him in January 1423 with the vacant electoral duchy of Saxe-Wittenberg. In 1409 he and his brother William founded the university of Leipzig for German students leaving Prague. His Saxon army was nearly destroyed at Aussig in 1426, and he died at Altenburg in January 1428. His lasting mark is winning the electorate for the Wettins.
britannica-1911-frederick-ii-elector-of-:
Frederick II (1411-1464), called the Mild, elector and duke of Saxony, was born on 22 August 1411, eldest son of Frederick I. He succeeded in 1428, sharing the family lands with three brothers, and at once had to defend Saxony against the Hussites. Clear of them by about 1432, he gained the burgraviate of Meissen in 1439 and part of Lower Lusatia.

In 1438 his right to cast the Saxon electoral vote was upheld, and he helped seat Albert II and then Frederick III on the German throne. Inheriting Thuringia lands in 1440, he and his brother William quarrelled over the division and fought a wasting war from 1446 until peace in 1451 left William Thuringia and Frederick Altenburg. He died at Leipzig in 1464. The entry closes with the Prinzenraub of 1455, when a knight stole his sons Ernest and Albert and was caught on the road to Bohemia.
britannica-1911-frederick-iii-elector-of:
Frederick III (1463-1525), called the Wise, elector of Saxony, was born at Torgau, eldest son of Ernest, and succeeded his father in 1486. He pressed reform on King Maximilian and in 1500 presided over the new council of regency. A friend of learning, he founded the university of Wittenberg in 1502 and placed Luther and Melanchthon in its chairs.

Though he stayed in the old faith all his life, and had made the Jerusalem pilgrimage in 1493, Frederick shielded the reformer. In 1520 he refused to enforce the papal bull ordering Luther books burned. In 1521, after the diet of Worms put Luther under the ban, he had him carried off to the Wartburg castle for safety. In 1519 he refused bribes from rival candidates for the throne, declined the crown himself, and helped elect Charles V. He died unmarried in May 1525.
britannica-1911-friedland-germany: Friedland is the name of seven German towns, and the entry treats the most important of them, in the grand duchy of Mecklenburg-Strelitz. It stands on the Mühlenteich, 35 miles north-east of Strelitz on the railway to Neu-Brandenburg, and has about 7000 people. The town possesses a fine Gothic church and a gymnasium. Its works make woollen and linen cloth, leather, and tobacco. Friedland was founded in 1244 by the margraves John and Otto III of Brandenburg. The entry is a short gazetteer note.
britannica-1911-froude-james-anthony:
James Anthony Froude (1818-1894), English historian, was born at Dartington in Devon on 23 April 1818, son of the archdeacon of Totnes. At Westminster and Oriel College, Oxford, he fell in with the High Church revival. He helped Newman on the Lives of the English Saints and was ordained deacon in 1845. By then his views were already turning under the influence of Carlyle.

The turn showed in Shadows of the Clouds in 1847 and the Nemesis of Faith a year later, and he resigned his fellowship to live by writing. His History of England from the Fall of Wolsey to the Defeat of the Spanish Armada ran from 1856 to 1870. It won fame for its style and dramatic character work. The entry also charges it with prejudice and careless fact, above all in overpraising Henry VIII. Lord Carnarvon sent him to South Africa in 1874 and 1875 to promote confederation, a mission judged a failure.
britannica-1911-gascony: Gascony was an old province in the south-west of France. It took its name from the Vascones, a Spanish tribe that crossed the Pyrenees in 580 and 587. The hosted text breaks off early, so only the opening of the 1911 Britannica entry survives here. It says the district was the Roman Novempopulana. Basque took root only in high Pyrenean valleys, while Latin speech held the plains. In the 7th century the name Vasconia replaced Novempopulana. The fragment ends with the Vascones under their own dukes, in name under Merovingian kings.
britannica-1911-george-king-of-saxony:
George, king of Saxony, who lived from 1832 to 1904, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the youngest son of King John of Saxony and Queen Amelia. Born at Dresden on 8 August 1832, he received a careful scientific and military training from an early age. In 1846 he entered the active army as a lieutenant of artillery.

In 1849 and 1850 George was a student at the university of Bonn for a time. He soon returned to military life, for which he had a strong bent by nature. In the Austro Prussian War of 1866 he commanded a Saxon cavalry brigade in the field. In the war of 1870 and 1871 he first led a division, then succeeded to the supreme command of the Saxon army corps. His name is inseparably associated with that campaign in the text.
britannica-1911-gunny:
Gunny is a coarse cloth used for bags and sacking. Its name may derive from a plant name in Rumphius. It may come from gonia, a local name for Crotalaria juncea. Knox's Ceylon gives one early notice of the term. He used it for cloth made from coconut husk fibre. Later usage ties the word mainly to jute.

Bengal's jute districts made gunny in almost every household. Warden's Linen Trade describes that domestic manufacture at length. Men, women and children all spun gunny twist. They used a thigh-turned spindle and a reel. Lower-caste women wove much of the cloth at home. It served for clothing, bedding and pack-sheets. Rice and sugar bags were a standard product. Dundee still made some gunny on hand looms.
britannica-1911-hamilton-anthony:
Anthony Hamilton (1646–1720) was a French classical author. He was born about 1646, in Ireland by most accounts. His father headed a Scottish Hamilton family line. His mother was the duke of Ormonde's sister. From age four to fourteen he was raised in France. His family had fled there after Charles I's execution. Catholicism barred the promotion he might have expected at the Restoration.

He served in the French army instead. His sister Elizabeth married the comte de Gramont. James II gave him an Irish regiment and Limerick's governorship. The Boyne's disaster exiled him to France again. At St Germain and Sceaux he found his true home. The duchesse du Maine favoured him especially. There he wrote the Mémoires du comte de Gramont. That chronicle of Charles II's courtiers made him famous. He died at St Germain-en-Laye in 1720.
britannica-1911-hope-anthony:
Anthony Hope was the pen name of Anthony Hope Hawkins, a British novelist. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists his rise and chief books. He was born in London in February 1863. He studied at Marlborough and at Balliol College, Oxford.

Hope trained for the bar, then turned to tales and sketches. His first novel came out in 1890, with more close behind. Fame struck in May 1894 with The Prisoner of Zenda. That tale of a false king set a fashion for Ruritanian romance. A stage version spread his name still wider. The Dolly Dialogues, out the same year, led a school of drawing room comedy. A sequel to Zenda followed in 1898.
britannica-1911-hort-fenton-john-anthony:
Fenton John Anthony Hort, an English theologian who lived from 1828 to 1892, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in Dublin, he was the great grandson of an archbishop of Tuam. In 1846 he moved from Rugby school to Trinity College, Cambridge. There he met three men who became lifelong friends and fellow workers.

The entry says Hort took his degree in 1850, third in the classical honours list, and became a fellow in 1852. In 1854 he helped found a journal of classical and sacred language study. He had been raised in strict evangelical teaching, but Rugby and later friends moved him toward a more liberal view. In 1857 he married and took a college living in Hertfordshire, where he stayed fifteen years.
britannica-1911-hudson-s-bay-company:
The Hudson's Bay Company is a firm set up to bring furs and skins into Great Britain. It gains them chiefly by barter from the native peoples of British North America. Its full style is the Governor and Company of Adventurers of England trading into Hudson's Bay. Its posts dot a vast region bounded by two oceans. The Arctic Ocean bounds it on the north and the United States on the south.

Furs go from the posts to Hudson Bay and the Labrador coast for shipment to England in the firm's own ships. Some go by steamboat or rail to ports such as Montreal for shipment to London, where they are sold at auction. Charles II granted the firm's charter in 1670. Prince Rupert and seventeen other nobles and gentlemen were named in it as the first company.
britannica-1911-john-elector-of-saxony:
John the Steadfast (1468–1532), elector of Saxony, was the fourth son of the elector Ernest, born on the 30th of June 1468. When his eldest brother became elector in 1486, John received part of the family lands. He served the German king Maximilian I in several campaigns, and he was an early follower of Luther.

On his brother's death in May 1525 he became elector and stood out among the Reformers. He helped put down the rising led by Thomas Münzer. He then helped Philip of Hesse found the league of Gotha in 1526 to protect the reforming party. He signed the protest at Spires in 1529, making him one of the first Protestants, and signed the confession of Augsburg in 1530. He joined the league of Schmalkalden and died on the 16th of August 1532. His elder son John Frederick succeeded him.
britannica-1911-john-frederick-duke-of-s:
John Frederick (1529–1595), called the Middle, was a duke of Saxony born at Torgau on the 8th of January 1529. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells how his father lost the Saxon electorate to the emperor Charles the Fifth in 1547. The young duke governed what was left to his house until his father's release in 1552.

From 1565 he ruled Gotha and Weimar, a fierce Lutheran whose one aim was winning back the electoral rank. He lent his court to Wilhelm von Grumbach, who promised to regain that rank and even the Empire itself. Warnings from the emperor went unheeded, and in 1566 the duke was put under the ban of the Empire. Gotha fell in April 1567 after a mutiny, and John Frederick stayed a prisoner until his death in 1595.
britannica-1911-joigny:
Joigny is a town of central France in the department of Yonne. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it 18 miles north of Auxerre by rail. Its count in 1906 was 4,888 souls in the town. It climbs the flank of a hill called the Cote St Jacques. Below it flows the river Yonne on its way north.

Streets in the town are steep and narrow, the entry notes. Old houses with carved wood fronts line those lanes in number. The church of St Jean holds a marble Holy Sepulchre of rare age. St Andre church shows a fine carved portal of the Renaissance. A gate with two vast towers recalls the old castle walls.
britannica-1911-letterkenny:
Letterkenny is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a market town of Ireland. It lies in county Donegal, west of Londonderry by rail. A count from 1901 gives the town 2370 people. It has a harbour at Port Ballyrane, one mile distant. In the market square a considerable trade is prosecuted. That trade runs in grain, flax, and provisions. Rope making and shirt making are industries of the town.

The Roman Catholic cathedral for the diocese of Raphoe stands there. It occupies a commanding site above the town. It contains carving from Rome and glass from Munich. It was consecrated in the year 1901. A Catholic college dedicated to Saint Eunan stands in the town. The town is a centre for visitors to the county. Its name signifies the hill of the O'Cannanans. That family lorded over Tyrconnell before the O'Donnells.
britannica-1911-marburg-germany:
Marburg is an old college town in Germany, set on the slope of a hill on the right bank of a river. The 1911 Britannica entry gives its rail span from Frankfurt and its town count in the early years of the age. Two bridges span the river to a suburb and the rail stop on the far bank.

The hill is crowned by a vast old castle in the Gothic style, once the seat of the landgraves of the state. Its knights hall and fine small chapel are the gems of the place. The castle now holds the prized state records of the land. But the true jewel of the town, the entry says, is its great church in pure early Gothic style, raised to hold the tomb of a saint queen.
britannica-1911-matilda-countess-of-tusc:
Matilda, Countess of Tuscany, known as the Great Countess, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica article. She lived from 1046 to 1115 and came from a noble Lombard family. Her father, Boniface, held Tuscany, Spoleto, Parma, and other lands. When he was killed in 1052, and her brother and sister soon died, Matilda was left at age nine as sole heir to the richest estate in Italy.

The article traces her fine schooling under her mother, Beatrice of Bar. It then follows her long stand on the side of the popes. For more than thirty years she backed Gregory the Seventh and the popes who came after him. Their foe was the emperor, in the great fight over who could name bishops. Readers get a life that shows how much land and faith could shape power in her age.
britannica-1911-mokshany:
Mokshany is the subject of a town entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was a town of Russia in the government of Penza, north west of the city of Penza. The entry gives its population in nineteen hundred as over ten thousand. Its people worked in farming or in local mills and works.

Flour mills, oil works, tanneries, and potash works are all named. The town was built in fifteen thirty five as a fort, the entry says. It was meant to guard the country from raids by Tatars and Kalmucks. It is thought to stand on the site of a far older town named in records from the ninth century.
britannica-1911-mulligatawny: Mulligatawny is a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica that defines a well known soup. The name comes from the Tamil words milagu-tannir, which mean pepper water. The entry describes a hot East Indian soup made with curry powder and strong seasoning. It was most often served with rice. The whole entry is a single short note, so it gives the origin of the name and the basic makeup of the dish, and little more.
britannica-1911-ohio-company:
Ohio Company is a history article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about two firms formed to settle the Ohio Valley. Both date from the 1700s. Each sought land along the Ohio river for new towns and trade.

The first firm was set up in 1749 by men of Virginia and England. George the Second backed a grant of 500,000 acres north west of the Ohio. In 1750 a skilled woodsman scouted the valley for the firm as far as the Scioto river. War for freedom stopped the work, and nothing came of the plan. The second firm, formed at Boston in 1786, had better luck. Its agents won from Congress a vast grant at a low price per acre. Its terms helped bar slavery from the North West lands.
britannica-1911-paeony:
Paeony, a plant kind famed for large bright blooms, is the topic of a garden entry in the 1911 Britannica. Two sets stand apart in the text. One set grows strong on thick roots with stems that die back each year. The other set, the tree paeony, keeps stiff half wood stems from year to year. The first set springs from two wild kinds, and the tree set from a Chinese kind.

Garden forms grow two to three feet high with large cut leaves. They bloom in May and June and suit large beds and shrub fronts. Rich wet loam and feed suit them best, the text says. They hate to be moved or split too oft. Old kinds bear Latin names in a long list. Tree forms can reach six to eight feet with blooms in hues from white to rose.
britannica-1911-panizzi-sir-anthony:
Sir Anthony Panizzi, who lived from 1797 to 1879, was an Italian-born librarian who made his career in England. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born at Brescello in Modena on the sixteenth of September 1797. He took a law degree at Parma and worked as an advocate. His part in a plot of 1821 against the duke forced him to flee for his life. He reached England in May 1823 with next to nothing.

Panizzi taught Italian in Liverpool and then held a chair of Italian in London from 1828. In 1831 he gained a post at the British Museum as an extra assistant librarian. He rose from there to shape the great library. The article also praises his edition of the Orlando innamorato of Boiardo. That work brought a fine Italian poet back from three centuries of neglect.
britannica-1911-poniatowski-joseph-antho:
Poniatowski is the name of a Polish princely family, and its rise is traced in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica under the heading of Joseph Anthony. The hosted page opens with the tail of an entry on a dagger, and then the family article starts. The house was of Italian stock. It traced its line to Giuseppe Torelli, who wed an heiress of the Lithuanian house of Poniator about 1650 and took her name.

The first of the name to stand out was Stanislaus, born in 1677. He joined the party of Leszczynski and rose to major-general in the army of Charles the Twelfth of Sweden. After the defeat at Pultowa he got the king safe across the Dnieper. He was sent to Constantinople and won a pledge from the sultan to march on Moscow. Later he made peace with King Augustus and became grand treasurer of Lithuania in 1724.
britannica-1911-potsdam-germany:
Potsdam is a town of Germany, capital of the Prussian province of Brandenburg, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes this royal residence town. It stands on the river Havel, sixteen miles south-west of Berlin, with 61,414 people in 1905. Lakes formed by the river link it to the capital by steamboat.

The entry places most of the town on the right bank, joined by a long bridge to the Teltow suburb. At the bridge's north end rises the royal palace, a great four-sided building of the seventeenth century, full of relics of Frederick the Great, who made it his favorite home. It also holds memories of Voltaire, who lived there for some years.
britannica-1911-reichenbach-saxony: Reichenbach is a town in Saxony, set in hilly land south west of Zwickau. Rail lines for three towns meet there. Its folk count past twenty-four thousand in nineteen five. A fine town hall from eighteen thirty-three and a hall of wild lore are its builds. Cloth, gear, and coach work fill its shops, plus dye and bleach work. It is first named in a writ of twelve twelve. Wool work came in the fifteenth century and took the place of mine work.
britannica-1911-scrutiny:
Scrutiny means a careful search or inquiry, and the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives the word a short entry with three set uses. The word comes through French from a Latin verb meaning to search or examine in full. In the early church, a scrutiny was the test of those being taught the faith before baptism.

Such folk learned the creed and the Lord's Prayer, were examined on them, and were cleared of evil before the rite. The days set for this varied from three to seven. When infant baptism at any time grew usual, from about the eleven hundreds, the scrutiny was folded into the baptism itself. The word also names one way of electing a pope, set against acclamation and accession. In election law, a scrutiny is the close check of votes that follows a petition by the losing side.
britannica-1911-simony:
Simony is an offence against the law of the church, defined in detail in the entry. Its name is taken from Simon Magus, a figure of the early church. In canon law the word bears a wider sense than in English law. One old definition calls it a willed act of selling things that are spiritual. Payment is made in goods of a worldly kind for such things.

An early case is placed in the third century, in the buying of a bishop's seat. A rich woman is said to have bought the see of Carthage for her servant. Councils in East and West banned the offence from the fourth century on. Church law books treat the subject at length in set sections. A man who bought his orders faced loss of his post and rank. A monk guilty of the offence faced a stricter house.
britannica-1911-symphony:
Symphony, in the 1911 Britannica, is a music entry that tracks one word through three spans of time. The Greeks used it first for concord in sound, then for the perfect gaps of fourth, fifth, and octave. It could also name the art of singing in octaves. In Roman times it kept a broad sense of voices and instruments in accord, and it could mean a concert or even an instrument.

In the 17th century the word named sacred vocal works with instruments, such as the Symphoniae sacrae of Schütz. The chief modern sense is a sonata for orchestra. That form grew out of the opera overture of the mid 18th century, which took on sonata style in three movements. Mozart still used a symphony as an overture as a boy. With Haydn and the later Mozart the free symphony split off on its own.
britannica-1911-tunny:
Tunny is one of the largest fishes of the mackerel family, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica describes the fish and its fishery. It is set apart from its kin, the bonito and albacores, by much shorter pectoral fins. Its color is dark bluish above and greyish, spotted with silver, below.

The entry calls it a fish of the open sea that comes near shore in large shoals, within known areas, chasing pilchards and herrings. Its regular arrival on parts of the Mediterranean coast built a planned fishery carried on since Phoenician times. The greatest numbers were by then caught off northern Sicily, which supplied most of the preserved tunny sent abroad.
britannica-1911-tuscany:
Tuscany, called Toscana in Italian, is a division of Italy in the west of the central peninsula. It is bounded by Liguria and Emilia, by the Marches and Umbria, and by the sea. It holds eight provinces, from Arezzo and Florence to Pisa and Siena. Its area is about nine thousand three hundred square miles. Its people numbered more than two and a half million in nineteen o one.

Florence is the chief rail centre of the region, with lines to the north and to Rome. A coast line runs the full length of Tuscany from Rome to Genoa. Away from the coast the country is hilly, cut by spurs of the Apennines. Old lake beds form plains near Lucca, Florence, and Arezzo. The valley of the Arno is the most fertile part, its slopes highly farmed.
britannica-1911-wayne-anthony:
Anthony Wayne, an American soldier who lived from 1745 to 1796, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born in Chester county, Pennsylvania, he came of a Yorkshire family. As a boy he showed a marked bent toward a soldier's life. He was educated in Philadelphia and worked as a surveyor in Pennsylvania and Nova Scotia.

He married in 1766 and spent some years on his father's farm, holding minor offices. After 1774 he took an active part on patriotic committees. He raised and organised a Pennsylvania battalion of Continental troops. At its head he first served in Canada, during the retreat after the Quebec campaign. His fine conduct in a skirmish led to command of Ticonderoga for some months. In 1777 he was made a brigadier general.
britannica-1911-william-i-of-germany:
The 1911 Britannica article on William the First (1797-1888) opens with his birth at Berlin. He was king of Prussia and German emperor. He was the second son of Frederick William the Third. He was a delicate child. He grew into one of the most vigorous men in Germany. He had a strong love of order. He loved all things military.

The article follows his early career. He became a captain in 1813. He showed bravery at Bar-sur-Aube in 1814. He was a colonel at twenty. He studied the armies of Europe with care. In 1829 he married Augusta of Saxe-Weimar. From 1840 he stood as heir to the throne. He was conservative in politics. Yet in 1848 he allowed that some concessions were needed.
britannica-1911-william-ii-of-germany:
William the Second was king of Prussia and emperor of Germany. He was born at Berlin as the eldest child of the crown prince. His mother was a princess royal of Great Britain and Ireland. On his tenth birthday he was made a junior officer. He joined the first guard regiment of the realm.

The 1911 Britannica entry tracks his schooling at a town grammar school. It notes two years at a college town, then a life ruled by drill and camp. He rose to lead the guard horse troops in his mid twenties. The court air of arms shaped his views. He leaned to the stern royal faith of his grandfather and the great chancellor. He leaned less to the free views of his own parents. Till his fathers illness he took no part in the life of the state.
bunny-brown-and-his-sister-sue-and-their:
Bunny Brown and his sister Sue gain a Shetland pony in this Laura Lee Hope tale. Grosset and Dunlap put out the book at New York. Thelma Gooch drew the plates. Bunker Blue, the tall boy of the house, walks up the path as play starts on the side porch. Sue has just tucked her doll in a cracker-box bed.

Chapter heads mark the road: In the Ark, The Frightened Pony, and Looking for a Pony come first. A man both short and tall, in the book's joke name, stands in the run. First ride, a lost handkerchief of Sue's, and a new trick of Toby the pony fill the heart. The Brown pair meet each scrape at child scale, with home help near. The pony gives this book its own mark in Hope's long series for small readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-flav:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Flavigny describes a Benedictine house in Dijon's diocese, founded in 721, the first year of Thierry the Fourth's reign, by Widerad, who richly endowed it. The Gallia Christiana places the new house, under St. Prix of Clermont, on an older monastic site from Clovis' time, once under St. Peter.

Pope John the Eighth dedicated the new church about 877, after which St. Peter's patronage prevailed definitively. Flavigny's fame rested partly on its relics and partly on its monks' piety, and the house stood at its height in the eighth century under Abbot Manasses. Manasses, authorised by Charlemagne to found Corbigny, brought St. Prix's relics from Volvic to Flavigny.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-pont: The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Pontigny describes the second daughter of Cîteaux, on the Serain. Hildebert of Auxerre asked Cîteaux's St. Stephen for a monastery on a site he had chosen, and Stephen sent twelve monks in 1114 under Hugh of Mâcon. Their holy lives drew so many subjects that twenty-two monasteries arose in the first two abbots' lifetimes. Pontigny was known as a nursery of bishops and a refuge for great men, sheltering Canterbury archbishops Thomas, Stephen Langton and Edmund.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-savi:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Savigny describes a monastery on Normandy and Brittany's edge, founded by Vital de Mortain. Vital, a canon of St. Evroul, gave up his post for the hermit's life under Robert of Arbrissel, then withdrew to Savigny's forest in 1105 and built a hermitage.

Disciples soon gathered in such numbers that fit buildings rose, housing monks under St. Benedict's Rule, read much like the Cistercians' way. Rudolph, lord of Fougères, backed his grants in 1112, from which date the house counts its start. Savigny grew fast into one of France's most famed houses, and its founder and many later heads were made saints or blessed, St. Aymon best known among them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albany:
The Diocese of Albany covers a wide stretch of eastern New York State, including the counties of Albany, Columbia, Saratoga, and Schenectady and parts of others, across 10,419 square miles. Of its 852,471 people, about 180,030 were Catholics, mostly of Irish, German, or French-Canadian origin. The entry traces the diocese from its colonial beginnings through its American growth.

Its sections follow the early missions and first parishes, such as St. Peter's at Troy in 1826 and St. John's at Schenectady in 1830. They then follow the bishops who built the diocese, including Francis McNeirny, consecrated in 1872. Later sections name the gifts that funded schools and churches and close with statistics for 1906. The clergy then numbered 214, among them Franciscans, Augustinians, Redemptorists, and Salesians, with teaching brothers in its schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-albert-of-sax:
Albert of Saxony, also called Albert of Helmstädt, was a fourteenth-century philosopher nicknamed Albertus Parvus and Albertutius by the Italian scholastics. He passed his first examination at the University of Paris in 1351 and served as procurator and then rector of the university. He was still on its arts faculty in 1368, writing on Aristotle's work on the heavens and the world. He is often confused with a namesake who also taught at Paris.

All the works surviving under his name belong to Albert of Helmstädt, divided between logic and physics. Following his master Jean Buridan, he held that a projectile keeps moving because of an impetus, a push, put into it by the thrower. He likewise held that the heavens move by the impetus God gave them at creation. His favourite theory held earth and sea in balance, and his Treatise on Proportions went through eleven editions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-alimony:
Alimony, from Latin alimonia, nutriment, from alere, to nourish, is in common legal sense the court-ordered allowance a husband pays his wife living separately. It is also the allowance a former husband pays a divorced woman. Two kinds exist: alimony pendente lite, pending suit, and permanent alimony after suit. England's matrimonial jurisdiction once lay solely with ecclesiastical courts, which, despite common law making a wife's property her husband's on marriage, assigned separated wives part of his income.

Following canon law, those courts handled only separation suits, divorce a mensa et toro, and suits voiding marriage from the beginning. Pendente lite alimony could fall in either class, permanent alimony only in separation, since alimony, incidental to marriage, could not follow a void-from-the-beginning decree. A husband's non-payment exposed him to excommunication.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-archconfrater:
The Archconfraternity of the Holy Agony is an association honouring Christ's mental sufferings during his agony in the Garden of Gethsemane. Its object is to win, through those sufferings, peace for the church, defence of the faith, and an end to scourges, or afflictions. It also seeks a happy death for hardened sinners about to die, and spiritual aid for all in their death agony. It began as a confraternity in 1862 in Valfleury, France, founded by Antoine Nicolle, a Lazarist priest.

Pius IX enriched it with indulgences at the start. It was authorized in 1865 to affiliate other confraternities in the Lyons diocese. In 1873 it became an archconfraternity for all France, headquartered at the Lazarist mother house, 95 Rue de Sèvres, Paris.
