After two additions to its indulgences, Leo XIII in 1894 allowed its extension through the world. Joining requires only inscription on its register.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bernard-of-cl:
Bernard of Cluny, a twelfth-century Benedictine poet and satirist, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. His birth, homeland, and schooling are obscure, with claims for England, Morlaix in Brittany, and the Montpellier family all weighed. He is famed for his verses On the Contempt of the World, a long poem against the age's vices.

The poem does not march in order but eddies around two poles: the passing nature of earthly pleasure and the lasting joy of spiritual life. Vivid pictures of heaven and hell, in fierce and lofty diction, may have reached Dante. The entry presents a lyrical monk whose wrath and wonder still carry his verse.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bethany:
Bethany, a village of Palestine, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Fifteen furlongs east of Jerusalem, at the foot of the Mount of Olives, it goes unmentioned in the Old Testament. The New Testament makes it shine as Mary, Martha, and Lazarus's village, where Jesus often found hospitality.

There Jesus raised Lazarus to life, the great miracle tied to the place, and near it he ascended into heaven. Its name most likely means house of misery, though the Talmud derives it from house of dates. The entry joins geography, etymology, and Gospel memory in one short piece.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-calumny:
Calumny, from the Latin calvor, to use artifice or deceive, means in common use the unjust blackening of another's good name. It charges him with a crime or fault he did not commit. In general the sin is mortal, as detraction is, though it may be venial when the matter is trivial or deliberation lacking. Objectively it is mortal when it is meant to do serious harm to the person traduced.

Like one who wrongfully harms person or estate, the calumniator owes full reparation. He must retract his false words even at cost to his own name. He must also make good other losses his victim suffered, so far as he foresaw them. In canon law the oath of the parties to a suit, swearing good faith in bringing and defending the action, is called the oath of calumny.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ceremony:
Ceremony in liturgy is an outward action, gesture, or movement that goes with the prayers and public worship of God. To these the Council of Trent adds the objects used in saying the prayers, such as blessings, lights, incense, and vestments. Ceremony answers to man's twofold nature, intellectual and sensible. As Aquinas says, man owes God a twofold adoration: spiritual in the inward devotion of the soul, and corporal in the outward form of worship.

Ceremonies serve several ends. They embellish and adorn sacred functions. They stir respect, devotion, and religion in the faithful. They lead the illiterate more easily to knowledge of the mysteries. They show the dispositions needed to receive the sacraments worthily, and move the faithful to keep their obligations with greater docility. The totality of a religion's rites is called its cult.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-charles-huaul:
Charles Huault de Montmagny was the second French governor of Canada, born in France near the end of the sixteenth century and dead in the Antilles after 1651. Educated by the Jesuits, he joined the Order of Malta in 1622 and fought Muslims and African corsairs. Named to replace Champlain before the latter's death was even announced, he reached Quebec in June 1636. He rebuilt Fort St-Louis and laid out the city.

Under him rose the Jesuit College, the Ursuline monastery, and the Hôtel-Dieu of 1639. From the outset he pressed for converting the native peoples, and in 1636 the Sillery reduction began. When Maisonneuve arrived in autumn 1641 with forty colonists, Montmagny kept them and in spring escorted them personally to their goal. He also built Fort Richelieu, now Sorel, at the river's mouth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-congregation-:
George Cyprian Alston's entry covers the Congregation of Cluny, the earliest Benedictine reform to become practically a distinct order. It began at Cluny, northwest of Mâcon, where William the Pious, Duke of Aquitaine, founded an abbey in 910 and endowed it with his whole domain. He set Saint Berno of Gigny over it, launching a stricter Benedictine life. Benedict of Aniane's ideas from Aachen in 817 shaped the reform, whose chief departure was centralized government, foreign to Benedictine tradition.

The reform spread fast. For 250 years remarkable abbots ruled Cluny, marking Europe's history. After the twelfth century its power eased, and French wars harmed it sorely. Its abbey church ranked among the Middle Ages' wonders. Its library, for centuries among France's richest, stored vast manuscripts. Spirit and organization departed from tradition, yet monks stayed recognized as Benedictines. Alston draws on Bernard and Udalric of Cluny, Lorain, Champly, and Sackur.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-conrad-of-sax:
Stephen Donovan's entry follows Conrad of Saxony, also Saxo, Brunswick, or Holyinger. A Friar Minor and ascetical writer of uncertain birth, he died at Bologna in 1279. Holyinger is perhaps his family name. Some confuse him with another Conrad of Saxony who suffered for the Faith in 1284, but they were two distinct men, though of the same German province of the order. Conrad became provincial minister of Saxony in 1245 and ruled sixteen years with much zeal and prudence.

On his way to the 1279 general chapter, grievous illness struck him, and he died at Bologna that year. His writings include several sermons and the Speculum Beatae Mariae Virginis, at times wrongly attributed to Saint Bonaventure. The Friars Minor at Quaracchi recently edited the Speculum, and its preface sketches Conrad's life briefly while judging his other writings critically. Sources cite that Quaracchi edition of 1904 and the Analecta Franciscana volumes of 1887.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cornelius-o-d:
The entry treats Cornelius O'Devany, Conchobhar O'Duibheannaigh, Bishop of Down and Connor, Ireland. Born about 1532, he died at Dublin in 1612, New Style. A Donegal Franciscan, he was appointed bishop in Rome in 1582, consecrated 2 February 1583. In 1588 he was committed to Dublin Castle. Failing to convict him of any capital crime, Fitzwilliam sought authority to be rid of him.

He escaped arrest until mid-1611, when, almost eighty, he was taken confirming and recommitted to Dublin Castle. On 28 January 1612 a packed jury found him guilty of treason, and he was sentenced to die on 1 February, Old Style. Drawn to the gallows past lamenting Catholics, he kissed the gallows, exhorted constancy, then was thrown off and quartered. Patrick O'Loughran, a priest arrested at Cork, suffered with him. The people carried off relics, prayed all night, and next night exhumed him for Saint James's Churchyard.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cosmogony:
Cosmogony means an account of how the universe came to be, set against cosmology, the study of how the universe now works. Christian teaching answers with creation from nothing and providence guiding what followed. Modern science offers its own origin theories, while Genesis supplies the Mosaic account. This long entry surveys the ancient world's answers first.

Babylonian, Egyptian, Iranian, Indian, Phoenician, and Greek creation stories appear in turn, each quoted and weighed, before a summary draws their threads together. Norse and American origin tales close the survey. Readers meet gods rising from primeval waters, worlds shaped from chaos, and poets confessing that even heaven's seer may not know whence creation sprang.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-councils-of-a:
This reference entry follows a string of church councils held at Attigny, a royal residence near Vouziers in the Ardennes. It runs from the eighth century into the ninth. Meeting by meeting, it shows how bishops, kings, and popes used these assemblies to settle disputes, arrange penance, and discipline clergy and rulers alike.

Among the episodes it records are a 765 pact among bishops to pray and offer Masses for one another after death. At Charlemagne's 785 council, two conquered Saxon kings were baptized. In 822 Louis the Pious confessed his wrongs before bishops and Pope Paschal I. Later meetings judged a royal son accused of plotting against his father, and heard a bishop's appeal to Rome. The result is a compact chronicle of Frankish church politics.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-epiphany:
Epiphany is the feast of Christ's manifestation, and this long entry traces its names, history, and customs. It was known as theophany, day of lights, day of washing, feast of the three kings, and Twelfth Day. Among Syrians it was called denho, or up-going, tied to the rising light of Luke's gospel.

The feast began in the Eastern Church. A homily of Hippolytus on baptism is sometimes linked to it, though its link is doubtful. The first sure reference is in Clement of Alexandria, who notes curious attempts to date Christ's birth to 20 May. Basilideans celebrated his baptism on 15 Tybi, or 11 Tybi by some accounts. From such Eastern roots the feast spread west, gathering the visit of the Magi, the baptism, and the wedding at Cana into one day of showing forth.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-bauny:
Etienne Bauny, a theologian, was born in 1564 at Mouzon, Ardennes, France, and died on 3 December 1649 at Saint Pol de Léon. He entered the Society of Jesus on 20 July 1593. After teaching humanities and rhetoric, he rose to the chair of moral theology, which he held for sixteen years. For a time he was superior of the Jesuit residence at Pontoise.

Learning and holiness gave him a reputation that won the confidence of distinguished prelates. Cardinal de la Rochefoucauld chose him as spiritual director, and René de Rieux, Bishop of Léon, trusted him with his most delicate affairs. In moral theology he knew his subject profoundly, yet on many points he was too lenient. Jansenist anger at that leniency made him the target when Pascal and Arnauld charged the Jesuits with lax morality.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-franz-joseph-:
Franz Joseph Antony, born at Munster in Westphalia in 1790 and dead there in 1837, was a German church musician, choirmaster, and organist. Ordained priest, he became choirmaster at Munster Cathedral in 1819 and succeeded his father as organist in 1832. Besides songs he published four choral masses and two learned works that remain his monument. They are an archaeological and liturgical songbook of Gregorian chant in 1829, and a historical account of the origin and perfection of the organ in 1832.

The entry is short. But it places Antony among the nineteenth-century scholars who treated church music as history as well as art, tracing chant and organ building with erudition that later dictionaries of musicians still cite. His career, spent entirely in his native city, shows the quiet continuity of cathedral music, father to son at the organ loft.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-germany:
Germany, a vast national history, traces the German people from tribal beginnings to the new empire. Its opening sets two clashing principles, German individualism against Rome's all-embracing authority. It follows Arminius's fight for freedom in the Teutoburg Forest into the Germanic states that grew from Rome's wreck. Theodoric dreamed of a Mediterranean confederation under the law of nations, yet Roman principle prevailed there while individualist forces prepared the national idea.

Only after Rome's western fall could a great Frankish kingdom gather the old Teutonic stock. Clovis overthrew Roman Gaul and built a Germano-Romanic state, colonizing conquered tribes in Roman fashion. Language, shifting consonants, and tribal shrines long divided rather than united the Germans. They lacked even a common name until theodisk, meaning popular, appeared in the ninth century. The survey runs on through medieval empire, Reformation, and unification to the new German empire, treating church and state throughout.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gluttony:
Gluttony, from the Latin gluttire, to swallow or gulp down, is the excessive indulgence in food and drink. Its moral deformity lies in defying the order reason prescribes, which makes necessity the measure of eating and drinking. A Catholic Encyclopedia article sets out the five ways the Angelic Doctor names for this disorder.

The scholastic verse gives them as too soon, too expensively, too much, too eagerly, and too daintily. One who eats or drinks so as to injure health or unfit himself for his duties sins by gluttony. So does one who eats for mere pleasure alone. In general the sin is venial, but one who lives merely to eat and drink, whose god is his belly, or who gravely impairs his health, is guilty of mortal sin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-harmony:
Harmony, a concord of tones sounded together and the Greeks' general word for music, entered church chant only in the ninth century, though northern peoples may have sung in parts much earlier. The first added interval was a fourth below the melody, doubled at the octave to give a fifth above. Hucbald of St. Amand gave this organum its theory about 840 to 930.

Later centuries added contrary motion, the third as a consonance, the freely invented discant, and rules of counterpoint with measured notation, producing conductus, motet, and the perfected canon of the Netherland school. Through Palestrina's Roman school, melody still ruled and harmony followed its flow, resolving passing dissonance into rest, until the seventeenth century began to free individual feeling from the chant's diatonic reign.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hugh-of-flavi:
Hugh of Flavigny was a Benedictine monk and historian, born about 1064, probably at Verdun, and dead before the middle of the twelfth century. Of a prominent family, he was schooled at St. Vannes in Verdun, where he took the novice's habit. When his abbot, a papal supporter, fled the emperor's bishop Dietrich and his antipope Clement III, Hugh followed him to St. Bénigne at Dijon.

At Dijon Hugh made his vows before Abbot Jarento, a strong friend of Gregory VII, and won the confidence of Jarento and of Archbishop Hugh of Lyons. In 1096, despite his youth, he was elected abbot of Flavigny. But disputes with the bishop of Autun and with his own monks, who would use even dishonest means for the pope, forced him twice to flee and finally to abdicate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-allarmet:
Jean Allarmet de Brogny, born at Brogny in Savoy in 1342 and dead at Rome in 1426, rose from herding swine to the cardinalate. Two monks, struck by the boy's ready answers, took him to Geneva and saw him schooled, finishing at Avignon. He then joined the Carthusians at Dijon, where his gifts soon drew notice.

Backed by the Avignon pope Clement VII, he became bishop of Viviers in 1380 and cardinal in 1385, later moving to Ostia-Velletri. At first he held the French obedience lawful, but by 1398 his orthodoxy turned him against it. He spent his later years working to end the schism that split the Western Church, a cause that shaped his whole public life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jean-levesque:
Jean Lévesque de Burigny, a French historian born at Reims in 1692 and dead in Paris in 1785. He began in 1713 with his brothers a twelve-folio manuscript dictionary of universal knowledge. At The Hague in 1718 he helped write Learned Europe in twelve volumes, contributing at least half.

Back in Paris, Burigny devoted himself to history and won rank as a careful scholar. Though sharing his age's philosophers' ideas, he was no extremist, but a modest, peace-loving man who wanted nothing beyond learning. His lives of Grotius and Erasmus hold facts found nowhere else, and his works range from papal authority and pagan theology to Sicily, Constantinople, Bossuet, and Du Perron.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-alexan:
Joseph-Alexander Martigny was a French country priest who became a pioneer of Christian archaeology. Born at Sauverny in 1808, he taught at the little seminary of Belley, served parishes at Cressy, Arbignieu, and Bâgé-le-Châtel, and became an honorary canon in 1849. Encouraged by his bishop and by the scholar Abbé Greppo, he gave his spare hours to the study of early Christian remains.

His Dictionnaire des antiquités chrétiennes, published in 1865 and revised in 1877, was the first work of its kind, gathering varied articles all written by this learned village priest. Scholars in England and Germany soon took it up as a model, and Martigny also issued a French edition of De Rossi's archaeological bulletin.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-sadoc-:
Joseph Sadoc Alemany was the first Archbishop of San Francisco. Born at Vich in Spain in 1814, he joined the Dominicans, was ordained at Viterbo in 1837, and spent ten years as a missionary in Ohio, Kentucky, and Tennessee, mastering English. Consecrated Bishop of Monterey in 1850, he moved to San Francisco as its first archbishop in 1853.

Alemany found only twenty-one adobe mission churches and a dozen priests in gold-rush California. He gathered priests and nuns, built churches and schools, and fought squatters and Mexico over church property and the Pious Fund. He resigned in 1884 and died in Spain in 1888, still a missionary at heart.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-karl-friedric:
Karl Friedrich Savigny was a diplomatist born at Berlin in 1814 and dead at Frankfurt in 1875. He was the son of the jurist Friedrich Karl von Savigny and Kunigunde Brentano, the poet Clemens Brentano's sister. His father was Protestant and his mother Catholic, and the children followed their mother's faith. Schooled at Berlin, Rome, and Naples, he read law at Berlin, Munich, and Paris, entering Prussian service in 1836.

He served at London, Dresden, and Lisbon, then as ambassador at Karlsruhe, where Bismarck credited his tact with winning Baden for Prussia. In 1864 he moved to the Frankfurt Diet, where his 1866 reform motion, rejected on 14 June, brought Prussia's withdrawal and the Austro-Prussian War. With Bismarck he made peace with the southern states and helped frame the North German Confederation's constitution.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-litany:
A litany is a form of prayer in which a leader speaks short petitions. The people answer each one, often with Kyrie eleison, Lord, have mercy. The entry roots the pattern in Psalm 136, where every verse ends with a repeated refrain. It also points to the song of the three youths in Daniel.

Eastern Masses, the Milan rite, and the Roman Missal all keep litanies. They range from Good Friday prayers for every class of people to the triple Kyrie of each Mass. The entry shows how one simple device, a spoken need met by a shared answer, grew into public worship, private devotion, and prayers for times of trouble.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ludolph-of-sa:
Ludolph of Saxony, called Ludolph the Carthusian, was a fourteenth-century devotional writer, dead on 13 April 1378. His birthplace is unsure, despite his name, and he may have come from Cologne or Mainz dioceses, then in Saxony province.

After thirty years as a Dominican, steeped, it may be, in Tauler and Suso, he entered the Strasbourg Charterhouse about 1340, governed the new Coblenz house, then resigned from scruple in 1348. His last thirty years passed in retreat at Mainz and Strasbourg. His Psalm commentary, popular across Germany, and his Vita Christi, a meditation on Christ's life rather than a plain biography, commend him still, though he never won public cult.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orders-of-sai:
Orders of Saint Anthony gather the many communities claiming Anthony the Hermit, father of monasticism, as patron or rule-giver. Disciples flocked to his Thebaid hermitage, some 6,000 by Rufinus's count, living apart or together under his word and example alone.

A rule drawn from Anthony's letters later shaped Eastern houses, though their actual rules reach only to Basil. Maronite Antonians split into Saint Isaiah and Saint Eliseus congregations, approved in 1740 and 1732, while Hospital Brothers of Saint Anthony, founded about 1095, nursed victims of Saint Anthony's fire. A rule under Anthony’s name was drawn from his letters and precepts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pardons-of-br:
Pardons of Brittany are the feasts of a church or chapel's patron saint, at which an indulgence is granted. Pardon comes from Latin perdonare, to forgive, shading through old French forms toward a gift. The pardons reach no farther east than Guingamp, whose feast falls on the first Sunday in July. They run from March to October, mostly between Easter and Michaelmas.

Five pardons stand out by kind. Saint Yves at Treguier is the pardon of the poor. Our Lady of Rumengol is the pardon of singers. Saint Jean-du-Doigt is the pardon of fire. Saint Ronan is the pardon of the mountain. Saint Anne de la Palude is the pardon of the sea. Largest crowds gather at Saint Jean-du-Doigt on 24 June and Saint Anne d'Auray on 24 July, the latter Brittany's most famous pilgrimage, with each parish known by its costume.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-peter-pazmany:
Peter Pázmány was the Hungarian cardinal who turned his country back toward Catholicism, dying in 1637. Born of Calvinist parents, he was drawn to the Church by his Catholic stepmother and Jesuit teachers, converted at thirteen, and entered the Jesuit novitiate at seventeen. After four years under Bellarmine at Rome, he taught at Graz, then rose through Turóc and Nyitra to Archbishop of Esztergom in 1616 and Cardinal Primate.

His pen fought Stephen Magyary's charge that Catholicism ruined Hungary, and his Hodoegus of 1613, part dogma and part polemic, argued the Catholic case unanswerably. He translated the Imitation of Christ, built seminaries and a college at Nagyszombat, and founded Hungary's first university there in 1635. As statesman he backed Ferdinand II and made peace with Bethlen in 1622. He was born in Protestant Hungary and died in a Catholic one.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saxony:
Saxony, in this entry, means first the Saxon tribe and then the land and kingdom that took its name. In third- and fourth-century Germany great tribal confederations replaced many small tribes: Alamanni, Bavarians, Thuringians, Franks, Frisians, and Saxons. Its long entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows a people from sea raiders to a modern kingdom.

Unlike the other confederations, ruled by kings, Saxons lived in independent bodies under chiefs, electing a duke only in war. At first a small tribe between the Elbe and Eider in Holstein, they took their name, it seems, from the sax, a stone knife. They fought westward until their name covered a confederation reaching almost to the Rhine. The entry then traces Saxon conversion, duchies, and the kingdom's church history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-scrutiny:
Scrutiny, Latin scrutinium from scrutari, to search or investigate, is a term used in several ways in canon law. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia begins with promotion to orders, where candidates must be examined, following Paul's warning not to lay hands hastily on any man. That practice is ancient, witnessed by Cyprian, who died in 258, in his thirty-eighth letter.

The ninth canon of Nicaea in 325 already assumes scrutiny of candidates in use, and many later synods enforced and defined it more exactly. Trent's discipline, in session twenty-three, chapter five on reform, orders a threefold scrutiny. First comes inquiry into the candidate's qualities by parish priest and teachers and by public proclamation in church, embodied in a testimonial letter to the bishop. A second scrutiny follows shortly before ordination through the bishop's own examination.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sejny:
Sejny, a diocese in the northwest of Russian Poland near East Prussia, began as the see of Wigry. Pius VI carved it out in 1798 from the diocese of Vilna after the first partition of Poland. This entry traces its seat at the Camaldolese monastery of Wigry, founded under King Jagiello in 1418. Its first bishop was the celebrated preacher Michael Francis Karpowicz. His successor, John Clement Golaszewski, enlarged the Wigry cathedral.

After the third partition gave the land to Russia, Pius VII reorganized the Polish church in 1818. He moved the see to Augustów, a city founded in 1561 by Sigismund Augustus. Its new cathedral opened that December. The entry closes with later bishops and the slow decline of monastic life under Russian rules against receiving novices.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simony:
Simony, named from Simon Magus in Acts chapter 8, is usually defined as a deliberate plan to buy or sell for a temporal price things spiritual or joined to spiritual things. Any exchange of spiritual for temporal goods counts, even where a motive of gain suffices without a formal price. Temporal advantages fall into three classes: gain by hand, meaning money and property; gain by tongue, meaning praise and support in high places; and gain by service, meaning undue homage.

Spiritual objects cover whatever serves the soul's eternal welfare, from grace and sacraments to sacramentals. The entry sorts borderline cases with care. A Mass stipend for the celebrant's support is lawful, but payment for the Mass itself is sinful. Chancery fees for dispensations are allowed, but payment for jurisdiction is not. Penalties close the article, from void benefices to excommunication.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-anthony:
St. Anthony was the founder of Christian monasticism, and this entry weighs the sources for his life with care. Its chief source is a Greek Life attributed to St. Athanasius, found in any edition of his works. Scholars now receive it with practical unanimity as a substantially historical record. They also judge it probably an authentic work of Athanasius.

Valuable supporting material comes from the Apophthegmata, chiefly sayings collected under Anthony's name, and from Cassian and Palladius. All that material may probably be accepted as substantially authentic. What Jerome's Life of St. Paul the Hermit relates about Anthony, by contrast, cannot be used for historical purposes. The entry gives readers both the hermit's story and the scholarship that tests it.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-lazarus-of:
Lazarus of Bethany, reputed first bishop of Marseilles, reaches Provence in the entry through a miraculous sea voyage. Tradition, combined across epochs, says Bethany's family, friends of Christ, with holy women and other disciples, were set adrift by Jews hostile to Christianity in a vessel lacking sails, oars, or helm. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 places their landing at the Saintes-Maries.

There the company scattered to preach across southeastern Gaul. Lazarus went to Marseilles, converted many inhabitants, and became their first pastor. Under Nero's first persecution he hid in a crypt, over which St.-Victor's abbey rose in the fifth century, and there he was buried after shedding blood for the faith. Under Domitian he was imprisoned and beheaded at a spot still believed to mark the place. The entry calls the whole a series of traditions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-vitalis-of:
Vitalis of Savigny, founder of Savigny's monastery and congregation in 1112, preached to outcasts from a hermit's forest life. Born at Tierceville near Bayeux about 1060 to 1065 to Rainfred and Rohais, he became after ordination chaplain to Robert of Mortain, the Conqueror's brother. Robert gave him a canonry at St Evroult in Mortain, founded in 1082.

Longing for a more perfect life, Vitalis gave up the canonry in 1095, settled at Dompierre nineteen miles east of Mortain, and joined the hermit colony of the forest of Craon. For seventeen years he lived ascetically, preaching with zeal, fearless speech, and tireless energy. He helped the outcasts gathering round him and reportedly tried to reconcile Henry I with Robert Curthose. He died at Savigny on 16 September 1122.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tuscany:
Tuscany is the central Italian region that matches the old land of Etruria. It takes in the provinces around Florence, Pisa, Siena, Arezzo, Grosseto, Livorno, and Massa. The entry gives its size and its population of nearly three million in 1911. It also sets out its church geography, with archdioceses at Florence, Pisa, and Siena and a string of smaller sees. Its story runs from Etruscan dominance and Roman conquest through medieval communes and feuding cities.

The narrative follows Florence's rise under the Medici, from bankers and republican rulers to hereditary dukes and then grand dukes of the whole region. It covers Cosimo I and his firm ordering of the state, the splendour and decay of his successors, and the later rule of the house of Lorraine. It ends with the region joining the new Kingdom of Italy in the nineteenth century.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-venerable-cha:
Charles Mahony was an Irish Franciscan priest executed at Ruthin in North Wales in August 1679. Born after 1639, he is known chiefly from a single printed sheet recording the last speeches of three priests executed that year, supplemented by Bishop Challoner's account. Mahony was seized while travelling to his native Ireland, driven by sea onto the Welsh coast.

At his trial at Denbigh he confessed himself a priest and was condemned, though, as his speech protested, he had never exercised his ministry in England before his capture. He forgave his judges, prayed for the king, and asked God to convert him to the Catholic faith. He suffered in his Franciscan habit, with great constancy, cut down alive and butchered according to sentence, as Challoner recalled from a manuscript he could no longer recover.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-vicariate-apo:
Northern Germany, or the Northern Missions, is a vicariate covering Mecklenburg, Schaumburg-Lippe, the Hanse towns Hamburg, Lübeck. Bremen, the Oldenburg principality of Lübeck, and Helgoland, under the permanent administration of the Bishop of Osnabrück. The wider missions also include the prefecture of Schleswig-Holstein, placed under a separate prelate in 1868.

Catholics numbered about 79,400 among nearly two million others, served by forty-seven secular priests in seventeen parishes and seventeen mission stations. With houses of Sisters of Mercy, Grey Nuns, Franciscan sisters, and Ursulines. Schleswig-Holstein added 35,900 Catholics in eleven parishes and thirty-one stations. In summer the flock swelled by 17,000 to 20,000 labourers, chiefly Poles, who returned home at winter's start.
charter-and-supplemental-charter-of-the-:
The Charter and Supplemental Charter of the Hudson's Bay Company prints the royal documents that created one of history's great trading firms. The original charter, granted by Charles the Second in 1670, names Prince Rupert and a company of London merchants and gentlemen as the body corporate.

Its purpose was an expedition to Hudson's Bay in north-west America, seeking a new passage to the South Sea and trade in furs, minerals and other commodities. The adventurers bore the whole cost themselves, and the charter gave their company governing rights over the lands and waters it entered. The supplemental charter that follows extends and confirms those powers. Readers of Canadian and commercial history will find here the legal root of a company that shaped a continent's fur trade.
crossroads-of-destiny:
A short tale of a changed past, by H. Beam Piper, fills this file. The text note says it was made from Fantastic Universe Science Fiction for July 1959. An editor's note recalls Piper's earlier tale of the diplomat Stephen Silk.

A history teacher tells the story in the first person. He still keeps a dollar bill in his bank box, proof he fears to show his college peers. In a club car he meets a man whose dress and talk point to a different United States. Its history, dress, and ways diverge from the ones the teacher knows. The tale asks what one small turn in the past could do to a whole land.
damn-a-book-of-calumny:
Short, stinging essays by H. L. Mencken fill Damn! A Book of Calumny, printed by the Philip Goodman Company of New York in 1918. This file is the third printing, under copyright of the same year. The contents list runs past forty pieces, most of them two or three pages long.

Pater Patriae opens the set, and pieces on artists, heroes, humour, and morals follow. Jews, Comstockery, eugenics, war, actors, and clubs all take their turn under his lash. Beethoven, Mozart, and zoos get essays too, beside free will and the root of religion. Mencken writes to provoke, and says so by his title. The book is a compact dose of his early manner, wit first and mercy last.
destiny:
A novel of ambition by Charles Neville Buck fills Destiny, issued by Grosset and Dunlap of New York under a 1916 copyright held by W. J. Watt and Company. Buck had won readers with The Call of the Cumberlands. Part one is named The Land of Promise.

Autumn in the White Mountains opens the tale, with children droning over their books in a crumbling school-house. Hamilton Burton stands at the centre of the later action, a man whose house politicians visit by night. Mr Ruferton and Mr Hendricks come to his door as the clock strikes nine in one such scene. Buck writes of mountain stock rising into money and power, and of what the rise costs.
frank-and-fanny:
Moore, writing as Mrs. Clara Moreton, tells a quiet rural story for the young. Her preface rejects exciting narratives and hairbreadth escapes on purpose. Gentleness, patience, and benevolence are the virtues she means to grow, through simple scenes of country life.

The schoolyard supplies the story's small cruelty. Jack Mills pins a taunting paper on Fanny's back and shouts names after the pair. When Fanny stoops to pick a flower, Jack's thrown stone strikes her face and draws blood. Frank's first impulse is pursuit, but he stays to learn how badly his sister is hurt. The book appeared at Boston in 1851.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-ImperialeAnthon: A United Press International item reports that Anthony Imperiale, described in the headline as a New Jersey white militant, sought a coalition of American rightists. Imperiale was a Newark figure who built his name on street patrols and hard-right politics. The surviving record gives the wire service and the headline claim but no date, so the piece stands as a UPI report on his organizing effort.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-MarshWAnthony_M: W. Anthony Marsh wrote this rebuttal in August 1983, answering Ramsey, the head of the National Academy of Sciences committee on ballistic acoustics. That committee had reviewed the acoustics evidence in the Kennedy case and rejected the finding of a likely second gunman. Marsh, an independent researcher, disputes the committee's work point by point. The file gives his title and position, but not the rebuttal's detailed arguments.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_cyber-va: Joint Task Force ARES was the United States Cyber Command unit built to fight the Islamic State online, and Operation GLOWING SYMPHONY was its main campaign. This Cyber Vault page presents the record of that internet war against ISIL. A companion Archive release covers Cyber Command's own after-action assessments of the same operation. The evidence here is the title alone, so this page works best as the overview entry, with the assessment documents supplying the graded details.
kenny:
Kenny is a novel by Leona Dalrymple, issued by Reilly and Britton, with a second printing in September 1917. Joseph Pierre Nuyttens illustrated it. Twenty-two chapters run from Brian Rebels to A Chronicle Concluded. The early titles name Kenny himself as the unsuccessful parent of his son Brian.

Joan enters in chapter three, and Adam Craig blackmails somebody in chapter four. A cabin in the pines, Kenny's truth crusade, and Samhain Night give the middle its color. Kenny finds the rainbow's end, becomes himself again, and faces a shadow of death. Dalrymple writes of an artist father whose charm and selfishness his son must outgrow. The Irish names and feast days flavor this family romance.
letters-of-pliny:
Pliny the Younger's letters offer a polished picture of Roman life. An introduction notes he was born at Como in 62 AD. His father died when Pliny was eight years old.

His uncle, Pliny the Elder, adopted and raised him. The elder Pliny wrote the famous Natural History. Young Pliny studied rhetoric under Quintilian and other noted teachers. He became the most eloquent pleader of his time, the introduction says. He also served as a military tribune in Syria. His letters imitate Cicero's style with care and pride. His account of Vesuvius erupting survives among these letters. That report remains the volcano's classic eyewitness record.
malvina-of-brittany:
Malvina of Brittany is a story collection by Jerome K. Jerome, headed by its title tale. A doctor narrates the preface and swears he never believed the story. Yet he claims it altered his whole outlook on life. Cousin Christopher gets mixed up in Malvina's strange affair.

Malvina is a lovely Breton girl with something of the fey about her. Love crosses the border of legend in her tale. Other stories here include 'The Street of the Blank Wall' and 'The Fawn Gloves.' Jerome writes in his mellowest, dreamiest mood. The book mixes Celtic twilight with his usual gentle humor. It shows a softer side of the Three Men in a Boat author.
my-four-years-in-germany:
James W. Gerard, America's envoy to Germany, tells of four hard years. He served at the Kaiser's imperial court until 1917. His foreword warns that Germany's power stands unbroken. He gives stark counts of men called, killed, and held.

Gerard says Americans do not grasp the war's vast scale. Five million prisoners are held across all lands, he notes. Pictures show court balls and his safe conduct home. The book was a wartime sensation when it appeared. It gives the view from the embassy as peace broke, talks failed, and America moved toward war.
over-strand-and-field-a-record-of-travel:
Gustave Flaubert traveled through Brittany as a young man. His friend Maxime Du Camp went with him. Over Strand and Field is the record, published in English at Chicago in 1904. Its first chapter is not Brittany at all. It is the Château de Chambord. The travelers walk empty galleries there. Spiders spin cobwebs over the salamanders of Francis the First.

Flaubert finds the château's poverty conscious and sad. It brushes its threadbare coat and tries to look respectable. One floor is repaired while the next rots. He retells its parade of owners. Gaston d'Orléans was exiled there. Louis the Fourteenth ruined the double staircase. Molière first staged Le Bourgeois gentilhomme under its crumbling ceilings. The young Flaubert already sees like the novelist he became.
podcast-dannyjones-q3i8X03minY:
Guitarist Vernon Reid, founder of the band Living Colour, warns Danny Jones that AI music tools like AI Drake are becoming a real problem. Fake songs in the voices of famous artists flooded the internet, and Reid sees danger for real musicians. The talk is about machines mimicking souls, as Reid puts it.

Reid explains what is lost when a program copies a singer's style without living the life behind it. He and Jones discuss credit, pay, and who owns a voice. They also ask what live playing still offers that code cannot. Musicians and fans get an artist's clear-eyed warning on fake art.
podcast-joerogan-fcdItgUjZnY:
Joe Rogan asks what goes on in the brain in a DMT trip in a segment from his show. DMT is the drug that fires a full dream world in mere minutes. Rogan is the show world's best known fan of the drug.

Rogan works through what scans and reports say the brain does at the peak of the trip. He weighs the view that the mind opens a door from the view that it just misfires in style. The segment is short and dense. Listeners get the science side of his pet topic. The library holds the file as an archive record.
richard-of-jamestown-a-story-of-the-virg:
James Otis tells the story of the Virginia colony through a child's eyes in this book for young readers. His foreword states the aim of the series: to show the home life of the colonists, not romance. Only facts a child would note are used, and the books are not sent out as histories.

The narrator is Richard Mutton, a lad of ten whose name stands in the list of those sent to Virginia by the London Company. He sailed on December 19, 1606, with the band of adventurers who founded the colony. London lads had teased him with Baa, baa, black sheep, and he explains how a boy came to join such a company.
roads-of-destiny:
O. Henry's short stories are gathered in this book of 1919, opening with the title tale, Roads of Destiny. Twenty-two stories fill the contents. The Guardian of the Accolade and The Discounters of Money follow, then The Enchanted Profile and a piece called Next to Reading Matter.

Art and the Bronco, Phoebe, and A Double-Dyed Deceiver show his range of place and trick. A Retrieved Reformation, one of his most retold tales, stands eleventh in the list. Friends in San Rosario and The Fourth in Salvador take the set south and abroad. Whistling Dick's Christmas Stocking and The Lonesome Road close a book of twists, rogues, and sudden turns.
samuel-brohl-and-company:
Victor Cherbuliez opens Samuel Brohl and Company at Chapter I with a thought on chance. Were events in this lower world governed by the reckoning of chances, Count Abel Larinski and Mlle. Antoinette Moriaz would almost surely never have met. Larinski lived in Vienna, in Austria. Antoinette had never been farther from Paris than Cormeilles, where she went each spring for the fine weather. Neither had ever heard of the other. Larinski's mind was filled with a gun of his own invention, which should have made his fortune and had not.

Larinski hoped his musket, a true masterpiece in his view, better in precision and range than any other known, would be adopted for the whole Austro-Hungarian infantry. A commission found merits in it, but three defects: it was too heavy, its breech choked too fast with oil, and it cost too much to make.
satanstoe-or-the-littlepage-manuscripts-:
J. Fenimore Cooper wrote Satanstoe as the first of his Littlepage Manuscripts, a set of linked tales about colonial New York. Its title page calls the book a tale of the colony and prints a Spenser line praising virtue and truth. The preface explains why Cooper valued old family papers of this kind.

Cooper argues that records of daily manners matter most when habits connect with larger principles. Grand causes, he says, get too much credit from historians, while small passions, motives, and plain chance do much of the work. Satanstoe tells Cornelius Littlepage's early career, courtship, and marriage in full. Later volumes follow his son Mordaunt and take up New York's anti-rent fight.
selections-from-the-writings-of-lord-dun:
Lord Dunsany's tales and play scenes fill this chosen volume of 1912. Contents list The Gods of the Mountain, a first act of King Argimenes and the Unknown Warrior, The Fall of Babbulkund, and Idle Days on the Yann. Strange gods, dream cities, and rivers of fancy mark the set.

Opening pages recall Lady Wilde and a Dublin crowd at the funeral of the poet Thomas Davis. That tale frames an age of Irish romance whose songs men sang at railway stations. Dunsany's own brief, jeweled prose follows, offering new readers a first door into his invented lands and their solemn, playful gods.
sowing-seeds-in-danny: Nellie L. McClung gives Sowing Seeds in Danny to her dear mother, under a verse motto on the art of being kind. The opening pages list the people of the story. Mrs. Burton Francis is a dreamy woman with fine theories, and her silent husband stands by. Camilla Rose, a capable young woman, runs the Francis home and now and then helps put the theories to work. The Watson family fills the rest of the list.
tacitus-on-germany:
Tacitus on Germany, in Thomas Gordon's English translation, comes from a 1910 New York edition by P. F. Collier and Son. An introductory note sketches the author: Tacitus was probably born about 54 A.D. and died after 117, a friend of the younger Pliny, an advocate and orator by training, who married the daughter of Agricola, the conqueror of Britain.

The note recalls that his Annals and Histories covered Rome from the death of Augustus to A.D. 96, much of it now lost. The short work here is his account of Germany: its situation, its inhabitants, and their character and customs. Roman readers met in it a hard, free people held up, in part, as a mirror to their own softening city.
tales-of-destiny:
Edmund Mitchell published Tales of Destiny in London in 1913, with the book first held under United States rights in 1912. Eight tales are framed as stories told by men of India, such as a Rajput chief, a tax collector, an astrologer, a fakir, and an Afghan general.

The first tale, The Maid of Jhalnagor, starts with the chief Rukpur Singh at the court of Akbar the Great. Other tales turn on stars, fate, love, and sacred things. Readers get linked stories where chance and fate shape lives, told in voices drawn from many walks of Indian life.
the-curlytops-at-uncle-frank-s-ranch-or-: Howard R. Garis wrote The Curlytops at Uncle Frank's Ranch, or Little Folks on Ponyback. Its contents open with chapters called Trouble's Tumble, Nicknack and Trouble, Off for the West, and The Collision, heading toward a place called Ring Ros- before the list breaks off. Only the title page and the start of the contents are present here, so the story itself does not appear.
the-duel-between-france-and-germany:
Charles Sumner's lecture The Duel Between France and Germany was given in Music Hall, Boston, on October 26, 1870, while the Franco-Prussian War still raged. Sumner calls the war a duel, and backs the word with Latin roots: Livy, Plautus, and Horace all used duel terms for war. He then asks what law should rule when kings fight.

War, he argues, is a duel writ large, and just as law curbed private duels, law should curb war. The speech pleads for courts between nations. It was reprinted from his Addresses on War.
the-house-of-dust-a-symphony:
Conrad Aiken shaped this long poem as a symphony in parts. He dedicated it to Jessie. Sections had already appeared in several journals. They include The North American Review, Poetry, and The Yale Review. One episode owes a debt to Lafcadio Hearn. It is The Screen Maiden in Part II. The opening movement begins at sundown. Lights go out window by window. Frosty sirens sound over the dark streets.

One figure moves through those streets again and again. He is an eternal asker of answers. He questions everyone's dreams. He drifts among the crowd like wind or music. The crowds pour through lamplit streets and climb stairs. They laugh and murmur as they go. The dreamer passes through them almost as a ghost. Aiken treats the modern city as a house of dust. Its people hold inward lives that stay half hidden.
the-influence-of-india-and-persia-on-the:
Arthur F. J. Remy wrote this study of German poetry. He had been a fellow in comparative philology at Columbia. The Columbia University Press published it in 1901. He dedicated it to three Columbia professors. The Iran scholar A. V. Williams Jackson was one. His preface begins from a familiar fact. An Oriental movement marked German writing in the last century. Every student of that literature knows it.

No one had studied the movement as a system, Remy says. His pages attempt that work. They trace how Indian and Persian verse shaped German poets. The notes warn of hard printing ahead. Marks crowd the text on many pages. Greek, Persian, and Arabic scripts appear. A dissertation on Germans reading the East needs that apparatus. Remy's book supplies it.
the-man-of-destiny:
Bernard Shaw's The Man of Destiny, dated 1898, is a play about the young Napoleon, and it opens with one of Shaw's long prose portraits instead of dialogue. The scene is Tavazzano, on the road from Lodi to Milan, on May 12, 1796. Two days earlier at Lodi the French, commanded by a general aged twenty-seven, rushed the fire-swept bridge while Napoleon assisted the cannonade with his own hands, artillery being his specialty.

Shaw's Napoleon does not understand the art of war, he says, but he has grasped one discovery: a cannon ball, striking a man, will kill him. To that he adds gifts for geography, calculation, prodigious work, and a clear knowledge of human nature in public affairs. Shaw calls him imaginative yet free of illusions, creative yet without religion, loyalty, or patriotism, though clever at playing on all three like an actor.
the-pleasures-of-a-single-life-or-the-mi:
The Pleasures of a Single Life, or The Miseries of Matrimony is a penny poem printed by H. Hills in Blackfriars, London, in 1709. Its title page says it was written on the occasion of the many divorces lately granted by Parliament. A second piece, The Choice, on the pleasures of a country life, is bound with it, dedicated to the beaus against the next vacation.

The verse speaks in the voice of a husband cursing wedlock as an uncomfortable state, cause of his woes and object of his hate. He remembers when he was free of those bonds. Business was no toil then, and each day brought new joys. Books were his companions, teaching wisdom in friendly silence. In his study he sat like a chief justice over dead authors' disputes, fearing no blame and desiring no bribe. Then he turned to maps to sail the globe on paper.
the-tale-of-benjamin-bunny:
Beatrix Potter published this picture tale with Frederick Warne in 1904, renewing the copyright in 1932, and dedicating it to the children of Sawrey from Old Mr. Bunny. One morning little Benjamin Bunny sits on a bank. He pricks his ears. He listens to the trit-trot of a pony. Mr. and Mrs. McGregor drive past in a gig. She wears her best bonnet.

As soon as they have passed, Benjamin slides down into the road. He sets off, hopping and skipping. He goes to call on his relations. They live in the wood behind Mr. McGregor's garden. In the neatest, sandiest hole of all live his aunt and his cousins Flopsy, Mopsy, Cotton-tail, and Peter, the cast for a sequel to Peter Rabbit's adventures.
the-white-company: Arthur Conan Doyle's White Company was published by Smith, Elder in London in 1891, and this copy came from the Hubbell and Smith working library. A dedication to the hope of the future union of the English-speaking race is dated 1891. The pages present here give the dedication and chapter headings, so the novel itself does not appear. Thirty-eight chapters run from a friendly greeting through monks, archers, and jousts. Later headings promise the sword of Spain, French castles, and a Basque ambush.
through-five-republics-on-horseback-bein:
G. Whitfield Ray, a pioneer missionary and government explorer, rode through five South American republics and published his wanderings in a twelfth revised edition at Cleveland in 1915. His preface quotes a missionary journal calling South America the darkest land. Ray thanks God for surviving hunger, thirst, and fever.

He hopes the accounts will stir missionary enterprise and sympathy for South American peoples. The Argentine consul-general ordered copies for his government, and German translation followed. Readers get horseback travel into unexplored interiors and visits to tribes Ray describes as untouched and unknown to outsiders.
william-of-germany: Nothing but the title page and contents is present here for Stanley Shaw's William of Germany, printed in 1913, so the life itself does not appear. Shaw was of Trinity College, Dublin, and the book has a frontispiece from a Berlin photograph. The contents trace the emperor from youth, 1859 to 1881, to his accession in 1888. Later chapters cover his court, the dropping of the pilot, and Morocco in 1905. A November storm of 1908 gets its own chapter. The list ends with the emperor of today, in 1913.
wisdom-and-destiny:
Maurice Maeterlinck wrote Wisdom and Destiny, turned into English by Alfred Sutro. Maeterlinck gave the book to Georgette Leblanc, saying her thought blends with his in it. An introduction tells the essay's odd growth. It was meant to run about twenty pages and take a fortnight. The seed idea grew and drew others to it, and the work held him for more than two years.

The result stands close to his Treasure of the Humble, the introduction says, but with a new aim. The poet who once chased beauty now probes the soul for truth. His finding, not his goal at the start, is that truth and happiness are one. Quiet, deep essays on how to live fill the book.
